title: Nigeria Is Open For Responsible Investments In Gas Sector, Says FG
body: The Federal Government says the country is willing to open its gas fields for meaningful investments as it continues in its bid to expand national gas consumption and bridge the gap between resources and the industries, power plants, businesses and households that need them. The Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas), Ekperikpe Ekpo, disclosed in his speech at the Association of Energy Correspondents of Nigeria (NAEC) Conference on Thursday, where he spoke on the theme ‘Access To Asset: Empowering Players & Driving Growth’. According to the Minister, the Federal Government has continued to prioritise critical gas infrastructure projects such as the AKK and OB3 Gas Pipelines, which are critical to strengthening the national gas network and connecting supply with major demand centres, to encourage more investments. Ekpo also noted that the government was also focused on enabling a conducive business atmosphere for investments. “We are also focused on creating a more attractive environment for investment. The reforms introduced under the Petroleum Industry Act 2021, together with targeted fiscal and regulatory measures for gas development, are intended to improve competitiveness, reduce barriers and enhance project bankability,” the minister said. “Our message to credible investors is clear: Nigeria is open for responsible investment in its gas sector.” He explained that FG realises the importance of collaborations with other stakeholders in terms of capital, technology and other resources. “We recognise that government cannot develop the sector alone. We need the capital, technology, expertise and commercial discipline of the private sector. “We also need stronger collaboration among regulators, financial institutions, development partners and industry players to ensure that viable gas projects can move from concept to final investment decision and, ultimately, production.” Ekpo noted that investments are not expected from just foreigners but also from local players. “Importantly, the opportunities created by our gas resources must not be limited to a few large players. We want to see greater participation by indigenous companies, independent producers, infrastructure developers, technology providers and emerging energy businesses. “Empowering more capable Nigerian players will deepen competition, strengthen local capacity and ensure that a greater share of the value created within the energy sector remains in the Nigerian economy,” Ekpo said. He emphasised that another major goal of the Federal Government was to improve gas utilisation nationwide, especially through the Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) initiative. The Minister also added that the gains of gas resources must translate to economic wealth for the masses. Our objective is also to maximise domestic gas utilisation. We must increasingly convert our gas resources into value-added products rather than viewing gas solely as a commodity for export. “Gas-to-power, LNG, LPG, CNG, fertiliser, petrochemicals and other gas-based industries offer enormous opportunities for investment, industrial development and job creation,” he said. “In this regard, the Government’s initiatives to expand LPG access and promote CNG adoption demonstrate our commitment to bringing the benefits of gas closer to ordinary Nigerians. “Our ambition is to ensure that gas is not simply produced in Nigeria but that Nigerians can use it, build businesses around it and benefit economically from it. We must equally ensure that access to assets translates into meaningful Nigerian participation and community development. “Nigerian Content must continue to evolve from participation in contracts to ownership of capabilities, technology, capital and assets. “Host communities must also see tangible benefits from petroleum operations. This is essential for building an industry that is sustainable, inclusive and supported by the people.” The Minister said FG will provide the policy certainty, regulatory clarity, infrastructure and enabling environment that allow investors and operators to succeed. “In return, we expect industry players to bring capital, innovation, efficiency and a commitment to developing Nigeria’s resources responsibly,” the Minister added. “The partnership between government and industry must therefore be built around a shared objective: turning Nigeria’s energy potential into measurable development.” He emphasised the need for the country to move from access to assets to development of assets. “Nigeria has the resources; what we need now is to unlock their full value. We must move from access to assets, to development of assets; from development to utilisation; and from utilisation to broad-based economic growth. “The Federal Government, under the leadership of His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, remains committed to creating the conditions for this transformation. “As we advance the Decade of Gas, I invite all stakeholders to work with us to build a gas sector that is investable, competitive, inclusive and capable of powering Nigeria’s next phase of growth. “Access to assets must ultimately become access to opportunity, prosperity and national development. I thank you, and God bless the Federal Republic of Nigeria,” he said. The post Nigeria Is Open For Responsible Investments In Gas Sector, Says FG appeared first on Channels Television .

title: London sanctions will not change Moscow’s course, Russian Embassy says
body:
LONDON, October 8. /TASS/. The latest British sanctions against Russia won't work to force Moscow to change its foreign policy course as intended, the Russian Embassy in the United Kingdom said in a comment provided to TASS.
"The latest batch of illegal anti-Russian restrictions targeting banks, individuals and merchant vessels only confirms that London has reached a dead end with its sanctions policy. Each new list is intended to demonstrate the UK authorities’ resolve, but in reality it highlights that the course they have chosen is ineffective and pointless," the comment said.
The Russian Embassy stressed that "Russia will not change its course." "Protecting national interests and ensuring sustainable development remain its unconditional priorities. Attempts to speak to us in the language of sanctions and threats are doomed to fail," the Russian Embassy added.
"London is seeking to cut other countries, particularly those in the Global South, off from Russian resources. This attempt to dictate terms exposes the self-serving and neo-colonial attitude of the British establishment towards the developing world," the comment highlighted.

title: NANS backs EFCC operations in Akure
body: By Adeola Badru The National Association of Nigerian Students (NANS) has expressed support for the operations of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), Ado-Ekiti Zonal Command, in Akure, Ondo State. In a statement signed by Adegoke Naheem Ademola, Chief of Staff to the President of NANS, on Thursday, the students’ body said it supported the EFCC’s mandate and efforts to combat financial crimes in the country. Ademola said NANS was committed to efforts aimed at promoting accountability and building a society where financial crimes were reduced. “NANS is not against the activities of the EFCC,” he said, adding that students, as stakeholders in nation-building, were opposed to fraud and financial crimes. He said the association recognised the statutory responsibilities of the EFCC to investigate and prosecute financial crimes, stressing the importance of compliance with the law. “To this end, we wish to state emphatically that we support operations of the EFCC, Ado-Ekiti Zonal Command, and we equally support the mandate of the Commission in its efforts to investigate, prevent and prosecute financial crimes and ensure that we have a society where financial crimes have no place,” he said. Ademola said the fight against financial crimes remained important to Nigeria’s development, adding that stronger accountability would contribute to public confidence in institutions. He said NANS would continue to support lawful efforts by the EFCC to tackle financial crimes and strengthen accountability across the country. “We therefore stand in support of every lawful effort by the EFCC to rid our society of financial crimes. “We believe that the Commission has an important role to play in strengthening accountability and ensuring that no individual is allowed to undermine the financial integrity of our nation,” Ademola said. The NANS Chief of Staff also stressed the importance of ensuring that law-enforcement activities were conducted in accordance with existing laws and regulations. “While we respect the lawful duties of security agencies, such duties must be carried out within the bounds of the law and with due regard to the safety and dignity of Nigerian students,” he said. NANS said its position was to support the fight against financial crimes while encouraging adherence to the rule of law. “We want a Nigeria where financial crimes have no place, where accountability is upheld, and where the law applies equally to every citizen,” Ademola said. The post NANS backs EFCC operations in Akure appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Our lifestyles may be killing us but our spatial planning is too
body: A few weeks ago, at the launch of World Heart Day 2026 at Korle Bu Teaching Hospital in Accra, the Director of the National Cardiothoracic Centre (NCC), Dr Kow Entsua-Mensah, made some pronouncements about “the growing threat of cardiovascular diseases,” which set a lot of Ghanaians on edge. Dr Entsua-Mensah cautioned that diabetes, high cholesterol, obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy diets, tobacco use and harmful alcohol consumption could progressively damage the cardiovascular system long before an individual became aware of the danger. He said the fight against cardiovascular diseases required collaboration among the government, healthcare institutions, corporate organisations, schools, workplaces, faith-based organisations, civil society and the media. Dr Entsua-Mensah’s revelation was a rude awakening that should shock all of us into a beeline for healthy living. What I find encouraging about the good doctor’s admonishment is the call for collaboration among all facets of society to cure the canker, because getting out of these health woods will require an assessment of our lifestyles in their totality. The plinth of my rant today is this: even though our lifestyles contribute hugely to what is happening with cardiovascular diseases, we as a society have not internalised the importance of healthy living, especially in our spatial planning. If you have ever tried brisk walking along our streets and neighbourhoods, you will realise that regular exercise was never a consideration when those streets were mapped and built. Any time one decides to engage in any form of outdoor exercise, one has to contend with narrow streets bursting at their seams with shops, hawkers, errant motorbikes and, lately, tricycles without side mirrors or any form of safety or warning mechanism. People actually get angry when you courteously ask them to step aside so you can pass. One time when I tried it, the retort I got was both funny and annoying. A gentleman (if he qualifies for that privilege) told me as I tried to pass: “After eating by heart, you are now concerned about your health.” If we stand any chance of curing this canker, we have to be deliberate about providing spaces where people can engage in outdoor exercise. Look around any fast-growing suburb and ask yourself a simple question: where exactly is a resident supposed to take a walk? Our estates are marvels of high walls, electric fencing and gates bigger than the houses they guard. What they lack are parks, walkways and open fields. The space that planners once set aside for recreation has a curious way of disappearing. One day it is a green patch on the layout; the next it has a container shop, a car wash, a church with a public address system and a signboard boldly declaring, “This Land Is Not For Sale.” By the time the neighbourhood realises it needs a place for children to run and adults to stretch, the open space has become a plot, the plot has become a building, and the building has become a very loud nightclub. The evidence that Ghanaians want to exercise is everywhere, if we care to look. Every Saturday at dawn, keep-fit clubs in matching T-shirts take to our highways and the Aburi Mountains, singing and jogging in formation while articulated trucks and impatient taxi drivers thunder past them. Some clubs have to arrange police escorts just to go for a run. Think about that for a moment: in our country, a person who simply wants to lower his/her blood pressure needs the same security arrangements as a visiting dignitary. That is not a fitness culture. That is a survival sport. Then there is the sidewalk, that endangered species of Ghanaian infrastructure. Where it exists at all, it has been converted into a furniture showroom, a mechanic’s workshop, a tomato market, or a parking lot for vehicles whose owners believe the pavement is an extension of their compound. The pedestrian, evicted from the space meant for him, is forced onto the road to compete with vehicles, or into a balancing act along the edge of an open gutter. One wrong step and your brisk walk ends not at home but at the emergency ward. We cannot tell people to walk for thirty minutes a day and then build cities where thirty minutes of walking is an extreme sport. Our spatial planning also shapes what we eat. At nearly every junction, lorry station and school gate, what is most readily available is fried, salted and sugared. Fresh fruit and vegetables are sold further away, often at prices that make the fried option look like financial wisdom. When the healthy choice is the harder, costlier and less convenient choice, we should not be surprised that many people do not make it. A city that places a fried-food stall at every corner and a fruit stall at none has, in effect, written a prescription, and it is not a healthy one. None of this is beyond fixing, and the fix does not require us to reinvent the wheel. We already have planning laws and a Land Use and Spatial Planning Authority. What we lack is the enforcement and the political will. The Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies must protect the open spaces on approved layouts as jealously as they collect property taxes. Every new estate should be required to provide parks and walkways before it is granted a permit, not promised them after the last house is sold. Every new road should come with a proper sidewalk and, where possible, a cycle lane, because a road built only for cars is half a road. Existing sidewalks must be reclaimed from traders and parked vehicles, with traders relocated to designated markets rather than simply chased away to return the next morning. Streetlights matter too; nobody will walk in the evening on a road so dark that they cannot tell a pothole from a python. Our schools must guard their playing fields against the temptation to sell them off or fill them with buildings, because a child who never learns to enjoy movement becomes an adult who never moves. Workplaces can encourage staff to walk, provide showers and give time for exercise without treating it as idleness. Our churches and mosques, many of which sit on large compounds that lie empty for most of the week, could open those grounds for community fitness activities. Here, too, the call for collaboration by Dr Entsua-Mensah makes perfect sense: the planner, the pastor, the headteacher, the employer and the assembly member all hold a piece of the solution. Of course, spatial planning is not a convenient scapegoat for personal choices. No town planner forced that third ball of kenkey down your throat, and no assembly bye-law requires you to wash down your ‘ waakye ’ with two bottles of sugary drink. We must each take responsibility, eat more vegetables and less salt, quit tobacco, drink responsibly, take the stairs instead of the lift, and, crucially, check our blood pressure and blood sugar regularly. Cardiovascular disease is a quiet thief; it rarely announces itself before it strikes. But personal responsibility works best when the environment makes the right choice the easy one. It is unfair to preach exercise to a population and then give it nowhere to exercise. As for the gentleman who mocked me on that narrow street, I have thought about his words many times since. He was right, in a way. I have indeed eaten by heart. But that is precisely why I would like to keep that heart beating, and I would appreciate a little space on the road to do so. If we get our planning right, perhaps the next generation will not have to dodge tricycles, hawkers and open gutters just to stay alive. Our lifestyles may be killing us, but our cities do not have to be accomplices. *** About the author; Benjamin Joe Danso is an Associate PR Director at Touchpoint Magna Carta.

New York is alleging that thousands of TikTok users, including kids and teens, were unknowingly given “ghost” versions of the platform’s safety features rather than the working versions. Reuters reports the allegation is part of an “updated, sealed version” of New York’s 2024 lawsuit against TikTok , which was “later ordered unsealed by a judge.”
According to the new allegations, TikTok’s “experiment” effectively blocked some users from accessing features like an option to reset your algorithm , which can potentially help users avoid harmful content popping up in their feed. As Reuters notes, users in the experiment “believed they had activated ​the feature, but their feeds did not change, unlike users who got the fully working version.” New York’s newly unsealed claims also allege TikTok ran other tests like this, like one Bloomberg reported earlier this year where TikTok allegedly withheld a safety update to its algorithm for some users.
TikTok spokesperson Nathaniel Brown said in a statement to The Verge , “We continuously make improvements to our platform which means that, like most companies, we regularly test new products and features to validate the experience and understand how they work in the real world.”
New York also claims that a product manager for Digital Well Being at TikTok internally raised concerns about the test, saying, “This feature is ​about algorithm transparency and control [...] A placebo group completely conflicts with that.”
The lawsuit claims TikTok misled users about the feature, as well, presenting Algo Refresh as a permanent reset, rather than a temporary one.

title: German defence group Rheinmetall doubles credit line to €1.5 billion ahead of expected growth
body: The new line replaces the previous €750 million facility. It is available to Rheinmetall for general corporate purposes. Rheinmetall also strategically realigned its group of main core banks. The group now includes additional international banking partners. The company said the new line creates additional financial leeway. It aligns the finance structure with the group’s expected growth at an early stage. Rheinmetall said the transaction strengthens long-term relationships with its existing main core banks. It also expands the banking network to include strategic partners. Credit line follows €500 million bond The renewal is another step in the development of the group’s financing. Rheinmetall placed a €500 million bond on the capital market in May 2026. The larger credit line broadens the company’s finance base. It also increases financial flexibility for the group’s future development. CFO cites growth trajectory “Rheinmetall is on a dynamic growth trajectory,” said Klaus Neumann, CFO of Rheinmetall AG. “By renewing and doubling our syndicated credit line ahead of schedule, we are creating additional financial leeway at an early stage for the Group’s further development.” “At the same time, we have further developed our group of main core banks and added strategic international partners,” Neumann said. “Following the successful bond issuance in May, this is a further important step towards consistently aligning our finance structure with Rheinmetall’s future growth.”

title: Uncrewed Systems Centre to pull drone buying together
body: The Uncrewed Systems Centre is the body expected to bring coherence to British drone procurement, and a newly arrived two-star officer has just taken it over, the Military Aviation Authority’s head of regulation and certification told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday. Commodore Neil Mathieson said the centre had not come up at the conference until that point, and that conversation about it tends to settle on the building it occupies when the value of it lies elsewhere. “The beauty of it is to cohere all these things, so we’re buying the right stuff with the right networks, with the right architectures,” he said. The task in front of it is considerable, and he described it plainly. “We’ve got British Army regiments out there who are operating four or five different types of drone. They then come together at brigade level with other regiments who have also got four or five different types of drones. They don’t talk to each other. They don’t communicate in the same webs and the same networks. They then get to division level, and you’re suddenly faced with hundreds of these things,” he said, adding that doctrine and policy have not yet caught up with the rate at which equipment is arriving. Speaking with his safety regulator hat off, he said the authority sees all of this and can advise on it while sitting outside the procurement chain. The same question arrives again further up the scale, he said, asking how a Royal Navy collaborative combat aircraft will talk to a Royal Air Force one. Companies telephone the authority announcing they will be flying at next year’s Steadfast Defender, at which point the useful questions are who is sponsoring them and how they intend to do it. Colonel Thomas Erlenbruch of the Bundeswehr’s Cyber and Information Domain Service made the same case from the German side, and put it in terms of what a soldier can reasonably be trained to do. He said: “Open interfaces are really, really important to be able to bring data from one system to the other, because we cannot forget that with all the autonomous systems, we also need a C2 system to get all the information they collect into, or to give missions to those systems for targeting. That’s one major user requirement, that I don’t have to train 50 different systems on the battlefield, but that I may be able to use one main system to be able to control all these different things out there, and that comes back to the standards and the interfaces. That’s the only way to be able to do it, because otherwise I cannot train my personnel to use it.” The post Uncrewed Systems Centre to pull drone buying together first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: 12 arrested as police seize firearms, suspected drugs in Tamale
body: Police in the Northern Region have arrested 12 people and seized firearms and suspected narcotics during a special operation in Tamale. The Northern Regional Special Operations Team, known locally as RED MARIA, carried out raids on Thursday 8 October at about 09:30 GMT in the Fuo and Kukuo areas of the city. Seven suspects were detained in Fuo for alleged drug use. In Kukuo, a further five people were arrested, including three found with weapons during searches of their rooms. Officers said they recovered two locally manufactured pistols, one pump-action gun, six sachets of Tramadol 250mg, and 25 wraps of suspected Indian hemp. All 12 suspects and the exhibits have been handed to the Regional Criminal Investigations Department and the Drug Law Enforcement Unit for further inquiries. A statement issued by police commended the team for the arrest. “We commend the RED MARIA team for this intelligence-led action, and we will ensure those arrested face prosecution through the courts,” the statement added. Police said they would provide further updates as investigations continue

title: Lagos records 1,324 fire, building-collapse, other emergency incidents in nine months
body:
The Lagos State Fire and Rescue Service says it responded to 1,324 emergency incidents between January and September, with fire calls accounting for 1,135 of the cases.
The agency revealed this in its third-quarter activity report, highlights of which spokesperson Maria Fadairo shared in a statement posted on Facebook on Thursday.
The report listed 79 rescue calls, 100 salvage operations, nine collapsed-building incidents and one gas-related explosion among the emergencies handled during the period.
Ms Fadairo explained that 210 people were rescued, while 65 suspected corpses were recovered from emergency scenes.
The service also recorded 341 false emergency calls.
The Controller-General of the service, Margaret Adeseye, noted that the figures highlighted the need for residents to take greater care as the dry season approaches.
“The statistics underscore the importance of sustained consciousness, prompt reporting of emergencies and strict compliance with fire-safety regulations across the State,” she said.
Ms Adeseye stressed that false emergency calls could delay firefighters responding to genuine emergencies.
The service estimated that property worth N79.44 billion was saved during the period, while losses were put at N13.24 billion. Property affected was valued at an estimated N92.68 billion.
January had the highest number of emergency incidents, with 203 cases, followed by March with 201.
September had the lowest, with 94 incidents.
March recorded the highest number of fire calls, with 176, while January had 173. September had the lowest number, with 80.
With the dry season approaching, Ms Adeseye advised residents to avoid indiscriminate burning and to exercise caution when storing or handling flammable materials.
She urged residents to switch off electrical appliances when they are not in use, avoid overloading sockets and ensure fire extinguishers are functional.
Property owners should also keep escape routes and access points clear to allow firefighters to reach buildings during emergencies, she said.
She urged residents to report fires promptly and cooperate with emergency responders at incident scenes.
The figures come against the backdrop of efforts by the Lagos government to strengthen its emergency response capacity.
In January, the government approved the recruitment of 150 additional firefighters.
Lagos has also recorded major fire incidents this year. In January, firefighters contained a warehouse fire in the Amuwo-Odofin Industrial Layout, where hundreds of 200-litre drums containing highly flammable materials were reportedly stored.
In 2024, the fire service reported 1,607 fire incidents in the state and estimated that property worth N117.12 billion was salvaged.
The service said it would continue with fire prevention, public education and enforcement of fire-safety standards across the state.

title: Koretsky: Challenging plenary week ahead, but financial stability, European integration must be ensured
body:
On the eve of the plenary week, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky said the Verkhovna Rada and the government share a common goal – to ensure the timely adoption of decisions necessary to fulfill Ukraine's international obligations and receive financial support from partners.
"Parliament and the government share a common task – to ensure the timely adoption of decisions necessary to fulfill Ukraine's international obligations and secure financial support from partners. On the eve of an important plenary week, a joint working meeting was held with the participation of members of the government and parliament. We agreed on the priorities for legislative work and the next steps for passing key bills," Koretsky said on Facebook.
The prime minister said this primarily concerns European integration initiatives and decisions within the framework of the Ukraine Facility, the IMF program, and other agreements with international partners.
"Not only does Ukraine's fulfillment of its commitments depend on their adoption, but so does the timely receipt of international financing. Given the challenging situation with public finances, this is one of our shared priorities. The Verkhovna Rada and the Cabinet of Ministers are coordinating efforts at all levels. We are continuing to work with relevant parliamentary committees, parliamentary factions, and groups to ensure that draft laws are properly reviewed and that the necessary explanations are provided for each of them," he added.
According to Koretsky, the Rada's plenary sessions will begin on October 12, during which the priority will be to consider the bills necessary for Ukraine to fulfill its international obligations, and, in parallel, the government is accelerating the fulfillment of its part of the commitments and must adopt all necessary decisions at the government level by October 15.
"We share a common understanding of the responsibility and importance of every decision. A challenging plenary week lies ahead, but our task remains the same: to ensure a result on which the country's financial stability, the European integration process, and the trust of our international partners depend," he said.

title: Maduro, his wife charged with conspiracy to commit torture
body:
NEW YORK, October 8. /TASS/. A federal grand jury in the Southern District of New York has approved an updated indictment against Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, charging them with conspiracy to commit torture.
"Nicolas Maduro Moros and Cilia Adela Flores De Maduro, the defendants <…> intentionally and knowingly combined, conspired, confederated, and agreed together and with each other to commit acts under the color of law, specifically intended to inflict severe physical and mental pain and suffering <…> upon another person," the document said.
One of the alleged purposes of such actions, prosecutors said, was "to repress and punish political opposition, silence dissent and perceived dissent, preserve and protect the power and authority of the members of the conspiracy."
In addition to conspiracy to commit torture, Maduro and Flores face four other counts: two counts of possession of automatic weapons and destructive devices, drug trafficking, and "narcoterrorism conspiracy."
On January 3, the United States attacked civilian and military sites in Venezuela, captured Maduro and his wife, and took them out of the country. Maduro and Flores appeared before the US District Court for the Southern District of New York on January 5. US authorities charged them with involvement in drug trafficking, but both pleaded not guilty. Delcy Rodriguez, who served as Venezuela’s executive vice president under Maduro, is currently serving as the country’s interim president.

title: Haaland wants Man City fans to ‘stay positive and stick together’ after guilty verdict
body: By Adegboyega Adeleye Manchester City forward Erling Haaland has urged the club’s fans to remain positive and “stick together” after the Premier League champions were found guilty of all charges relating to serious financial breaches. An independent commission found City guilty of all charges brought against them over alleged breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, with the club subsequently lodging an appeal against the verdict. City have maintained that they are “innocent”, describing the commission’s judgement as an “opinion” and claiming it contains “clear material errors, of law, principle and fact”. Speaking in an interview with Sky Sports, Haaland urged City supporters to stand by the club and look ahead despite the verdict. “They’re going to have a good time. “We have to stick together. We have to stay with each other, and we have to stay positive. No matter what happens in life, we always have to have a smile. “So we have to stay positive, look ahead, and try to win football games and try to enjoy the situation and win the game. “We have to stick together; we have to spread the love to each other. So yeah: stick together, and enjoy the ride and smile,” Haaland said. The independent commission found that between the 2009/10 and 2017/18 seasons, City arranged what it described as “sham” contracts with several commercial partners as part of a “disguised funding scheme” to artificially inflate the club’s revenues by £830 million. City have appealed the verdict. Haaland, who is the son of former Manchester City player Alf-Inge Haaland, also stressed his connection with the club and the city. “I care a lot about the city, I have to say. I care a lot about the fans because I’m a fan myself, and I feel with them as well,” he said. The Norway international also looked ahead to City’s Premier League clash with Liverpool, describing the fixture as special. “It’s always special to play against Liverpool. Especially with Pep and Klopp. I remember sitting in Salzburg and Dortmund and watching the games, how much they pushed each other. It’s always special games there. “I won there, I drew there, I lost. So it’s always special, and every Premier League game is different, and every game against Liverpool is always special.” City are scheduled to face Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday. title: US Embassy Issues Alert Over Potential Long-Range Attacks in Ethiopia
body: The US Embassy in Addis Ababa issued a security alert warning of potential long-range attacks in Ethiopia, citing reports of recent strikes against military installations as conflict intensifies across the country’s northern regions. In an alert published on October 7, the embassy advised US citizens to exercise extreme caution and follow guidance from local authorities. While the embassy did not specify which military facilities were targeted or their exact locations, it strongly advised against travel to the Amhara, Tigray, and Afar regions—including the historic town of Lalibela. US citizens currently in those areas were urged to shelter in place or depart safely if conditions allow. The security warning comes amid a resurgence of fighting in northern Ethiopia between federal forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) alongside affiliated groups. The renewed violence threatens the fragile peace established by the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which officially ended two years of devastating war. International bodies have raised alarm over the escalation. On September 23, the African Union (AU), which brokered the Pretoria peace talks, expressed deep concern over the military buildup and urged both parties to resume direct dialogue. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) similarly called for an immediate cessation of hostilities. United Nations officials have also warned of an escalating humanitarian crisis. UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged all parties to protect civilians and ensure unhindered humanitarian access. Meanwhile, Ozonnia Ojielo, the UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Ethiopia, reported that the fighting poses grave risks to civilians—particularly internally displaced persons—and noted increasing incidents targeting aid personnel, assets, and facilities. Although the embassy noted that the security situation in the capital, Addis Ababa, remains stable, it cautioned that ongoing conflict in the north could lead to broader disruptions, including potential internet and telecommunications blackouts.

title: Umahi lists completed roads, bridges under Tinubu
body: By John Alechenu, Abuja ABUJA — The Minister of Works, Engr. David Umahi, has listed federal roads and bridges completed under the administration of President Bola Tinubu and awaiting commissioning across the six geopolitical zones. Umahi disclosed this on Thursday in Abuja at a press conference on the four legacy road projects, ongoing interventions and completed projects being executed by the ministry. The minister said the administration had moved from planning to delivery, with several major road corridors either completed or at advanced stages of construction. According to him, the four legacy projects — the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway, Calabar-Ebonyi-Abuja Trans-Saharan corridor and the Akwanga-Jos-Bauchi-Gombe-Biu-Maiduguri dualisation — were strategic investments aimed at connecting the six geopolitical zones and driving economic growth. Coastal highway Giving an update on the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, Umahi said Section I, covering 47 kilometres, had been completed, while Section II, spanning about 55 kilometres, was nearing completion, with major flyovers, overpasses and underpasses incorporated into the project. He said sections around the Dangote Refinery and Lekki Deep Seaport had been redesigned to integrate rail, road and industrial infrastructure. The minister explained that the Ondo axis was also redesigned because of difficult terrain and deep pits. He added that President Tinubu had directed that the continuation of the Coastal Highway be aligned with the existing East-West Road in the Niger Delta, with critical sections raised to address flooding. On the Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway, Umahi said construction was progressing in Sokoto, Kebbi, Oyo, Ogun and Badagry, while work on the Niger and Kwara sections would commence soon. Projects ready for commissioning Umahi said the strongest evidence of the administration’s delivery was the number of completed projects awaiting commissioning. “We have quite a lot of projects. We have completed projects and we have ongoing projects. We are updating the compendium and it will be made available on the Ministry’s website,” he said. Among the projects he listed as completed and ready for commissioning were Section I of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway; 70km of the Kano-Maiduguri Road by Strabag; Kwanar Danja-Hadejia Road; Kaduna-Pambeguwa Road; and 43km of the Keffi-Mararaba Road executed by China Harbour. Others include the 15km Lafia Bypass on the 260km Makurdi-Numan Road; 7.9km Bodo-Bonny Road, including bridges across the Opobo Channel; and 15km of concrete pavement at Obajana on the Lokoja-Benin corridor. The minister also listed the 7.5km Danbatta-Demesu dualised road; Gombe-Potiskum rehabilitation; Azare Road linking Jigawa and Bauchi; five-span Apapa Bridge; the 23-span, 23km flyover at Eke Obinagu; and the three-span, 75-metre dualised Tizm Bridge in Enugu. Other completed projects, according to Umahi, include the 24km Shagamu Interchange to Iperu Junction and sections of the Lagos-Badagry and Lagos-Ibadan-Lagos-Shagamu-Ore corridors. He also listed the 375km Abuja-Kaduna-Zaria-Kano Expressway, saying all sections except the Jere-Kaduna section had been completed, while solar lighting was being installed to improve safety along the route. Umahi said the ministry was enforcing the use of concrete pavement on selected projects to improve durability, following due procurement processes through the Bureau of Public Procurement and the Federal Executive Council. He added that the ministry had launched “Operation Rescue” on the Benin-Asaba Expressway to restore mobility under a concrete reconstruction plan. The post Umahi lists completed roads, bridges under Tinubu appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Chamber of Mines challenges Reuters report on proposed mining law
body: The Ghana Chamber of Mines has challenged a Reuters report on the proposed Minerals and Mining Bill 2026, saying it lacks sufficient legal and policy context on provisions concerning the State’s special-share power and the duration of mining leases. In a rejoinder issued on October 7, 2026, the Chamber said it had reviewed a September 30 Reuters report titled “Ghana bill would give state special share rights in mining firms, draft shows.” It said the report did not make sufficiently clear that the special-share power already exists under Ghanaian law. According to the Chamber, Section 60 of the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703) gives the Minister the power, by written notice, to require a mining company to issue a special share to the Republic for no consideration. “The power has therefore been part of Ghana’s mining legislation since 2006,” the Chamber stated. It said the special share under Act 703 is a non-voting preference share and, unless otherwise agreed by the Minister and the company, does not provide rights to dividends, profits or company assets upon liquidation. The share does, however, carry consent rights in relation to specified major corporate transactions. The Chamber said Clause 57 of the proposed Bill largely carries forward this existing framework while increasing sanctions for non-compliance. It is therefore asking Reuters to clarify that the special-share power is not being introduced for the first time under the 2026 Bill, although the proposed legislation would re-enact the provision with revised sanctions. The Chamber also highlighted what it described as a difference between the published Bill and the government’s subsequent public position on the duration of mining leases. It acknowledged that Reuters accurately reported Clause 39(2)(a) of the May 2026 version of the Bill published by Parliament. That provision proposes an initial mining lease term of 15 years or the forecast life of the mine, whichever is shorter. However, the Chamber said this should be distinguished from a subsequent statement by the government on its intended policy position. At the Government Accountability Series on July 15, 2026, the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources said: “Mining lease period is now fixed at 20 years maximum.” The Chamber noted that the statement was made after the Bill had been laid before Parliament. It said the statement indicates the government’s subsequently stated policy intention but does not, by itself, amend the Bill unless Parliament changes the text during its consideration. “The material point for readers is the unresolved difference between the text published by Parliament and the Government’s later public statement,” the Chamber stated. The Chamber said it respects Reuters and other media organisations’ role in scrutinising legislation and informing the public and international investment community. It acknowledged that the Bill contains substantive proposals requiring careful examination but argued that reporting should distinguish between existing law, proposed legislative changes and subsequent government statements. The Chamber said such distinctions were particularly important because international reporting on Ghana’s mining sector is followed by investors, lenders, mining companies, analysts and policymakers. It has therefore asked Reuters to update its report to reflect that the special-share power already exists under Section 60 of Act 703 and to acknowledge the government’s July 15 statement on a proposed maximum 20-year mining lease term. The rejoinder was signed by Albert Amekudzi, External Relations and Sustainability Officer of the Ghana Chamber of Mines. The Minerals and Mining Bill 2026 is currently before Parliament and proposes reforms to Ghana’s mining sector, including provisions relating to state participation, local content and mining lease durations. The Chamber said it remains committed to engaging constructively on the Bill while supporting reforms aimed at strengthening governance, increasing Ghanaian participation and national value, and maintaining predictability for long-term mining investment. Reuters had not, at the time of the Chamber’s rejoinder, publicly responded to the request for an update to its report. 176 Rejoinder To Reuters Report On Ghana’s Draft _261008_130539 Download

title: Are you ready for everything to look like TikTok?
body:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A pair of tests on Facebook and Instagram offer a preview of what all social media could come to look like.﻿
A pair of tests on Facebook and Instagram offer a preview of what all social media could come to look like.﻿
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.
Since TikTok burst into mainstream consciousness, many things have been called a “TikTok clone”: YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels, Snapchat Spotlight, Netflix’s Clips, LinkedIn’s vertical video feed, and countless other, less recognizable names like Triller, Zynn, and Byte.
For years now, Facebook and Instagram have pumped users’ feeds with video as Meta chases TikTok’s runaway success. But if tests running abroad are any indication, the TikTok-ification of social media might finally be reaching its fullest form.
TechCrunch reports that some users in India are getting a Facebook test that, upon opening the app, drops them directly into an immersive, full-screen video feed. Meta hinted that this “experience” would be coming to “video-heavy countries” first, followed by a potential US expansion in 2027. At the same time, Romania-based app researcher Radu Oncescu noticed an option on Instagram to have Reels be the first thing a user sees when they open the app. Instagram Stories remain at the top of the feed, per screenshots from Oncescu, while swiping the screen pulls up the traditional feed of posts from accounts a user follows. Sound is on for Reels by default.
Meta spokesperson Devi Narasimhan told The Verge that the Instagram test is live in a handful of countries, but didn’t specify which. Users can switch back to the original layout, Narasimhan says, and Reels will be unmuted once a user swipes or clicks into a video.
There’s still a chance Instagram and Facebook won’t end up looking exactly like TikTok — not all tests become permanent features. But we have been barreling toward this for a long time, with some user pushback along the way that always seems to get ironed out. Video content made for quick consumption is clearly a priority for Meta. Even Threads, Meta’s text-based platform that reaches half a billion people every month, was barely mentioned in the company’s recent earnings call . What was mentioned? Time users spent watching videos on Facebook (up 9 percent globally and 10 percent in the US and Canada), improvements to the ranking system used for Reels, and ranking models that the company says can “identify high-quality new Reels at creation.”
TikTok’s — and by extension, its copycats’ — focus on video has reshaped all of the industries that depend upon such platforms for distribution. Podcasts have become videos, which have become clips . TV shows have become “microdramas” and movies have been chopped up into 50 parts . Political astroturfing has taken on the form of “user-generated content.” It’s not clear if users actually prefer video over text or images, or if they simply engage with it because it’s what social media platforms have placed directly in front of them — engagement is engagement, so platforms likely don’t care either way.
But as social media has turned video-focused, users report posting less online. Morning Consult polling found that while 81 percent of US respondents reported watching an Instagram Reel, only 39 percent say they’ve posted one. What happens when watching videos is the backbone of what we do online, yet relatively few people want to make them in the first place? This explains, at least in part, why platforms tolerate or even recommend AI slop content. Whether a slowdown in posting is because of the move to video is anyone’s guess, but it’s clear we have all become voyeurs.
The potential for Instagram and Facebook to become video feeds by default would be a seismic shift in form. But it would also mark the end of a more philosophical distinction: that these platforms are for keeping in touch with people. It was painful enough to ask writers, photographers, nonprofits, podcasters, and other creatives to spin up video content studios just to avoid being rendered invisible by the algorithm. It’s another to ask your aunt and old college roommate to do the same or get bumped onto a different page, easily forgotten. Time will tell if engagement is high enough for Meta to go forward with these tests in the US and other regions. If and when it does expand, at least we will have seen it coming.

title: State Police: Nigeria needs 554,353 personnel — Abiodun
body: …seeks take-off fund to prevent poorer states from being left behind By Adeola Badru IBADAN — Nigeria will require an additional 554,353 personnel to adequately staff the proposed State Police system, Chairman of the Southern Governors’ Forum and Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun, has said. Abiodun also called for the establishment of a dedicated State Police Take-Off Fund to ensure that disparities in the financial capacity of states do not undermine the proposed security architecture. The governor spoke on Thursday while delivering the keynote address at the posthumous 70th birthday colloquium of the late former Ondo State Governor, Oluwarotimi Akeredolu, at the International Conference Centre, University of Ibadan. The colloquium, organised under the theme, “Fundamentals and Governance of State Policing: Towards a New Architecture for National Security in Nigeria,” brought together governors, former governors, lawmakers, security chiefs, traditional rulers, academics, civil society actors, family members and associates of the late governor. Abiodun, who is also Chairman of the Nigeria Governors’ Forum Committee on State Police and a member of the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill, said State Police had moved beyond advocacy to a national imperative requiring urgent and practical implementation. According to him, data from the Nigeria Governors’ Forum, based on the United Nations ratio of one police officer to 414 citizens, indicated that Nigeria would require 554,353 additional State Police personnel, translating to about 184,784 recruits annually over three years. “The debate is no longer whether Nigeria needs State Police, but how swiftly and sustainably we establish it,” Abiodun said. He argued that the country could no longer sustain a security architecture in which virtually every policing responsibility was centralised in Abuja, stressing the need to bring policing closer to the people. “Security is intrinsically local. You cannot police a community whose language you do not speak, whose terrain you do not know. State policing is not a threat to unity; it is the bedrock of stability and prosperity,” he said. Funding challenge Abiodun, however, warned that the financial realities of the states must be addressed before the proposed policing structure could become effective. He said only five states — Lagos, Rivers, the Federal Capital Territory, Ogun and Enugu — accounted for 61.6 per cent of Internally Generated Revenue, while 76 per cent of states generated below the national average of N13,600 per capita, with half earning less than N6,334 per capita. He warned that the disparities could undermine the reform if the Federal Government and states failed to establish a financing mechanism that guaranteed minimum policing capacity across the federation. “Insecurity in low-revenue states spills over nationally. Underfunding one state’s police becomes everyone’s crisis,” he said. The governor therefore advocated a constitutional State Police Take-Off Fund based on equal-access grants, need-based top-ups and standards-linked disbursements. He argued that security should not become a function of the financial strength of the state in which a citizen resides. Abiodun said the Presidential Working Group was already developing operational blueprints, financial models, accountability mechanisms and legislative oversight arrangements for the proposed system, including frameworks for recruitment, training, governance and redress for abuses. He identified eight fundamentals that should underpin the State Police architecture: a clear legal framework; professional and merit-based recruitment and training; personnel welfare; predictable and sustainable funding; effective use of technology; safeguards against political abuse; deliberate community engagement; and coordination across state boundaries. The governor said recruitment must be transparent, properly vetted and representative, while officers must receive training in investigation, evidence handling, lawful arrest, conflict management, proportionate use of force and protection of vulnerable persons. He also insisted that political affiliation must not determine access to police protection. “Political opponents, journalists, peaceful protesters and minority communities deserve equal protection. “Disagreement with a government cannot diminish a citizen’s rights. We must earn public confidence through safeguards that work,” he said. Abiodun called for adequate welfare for personnel, including regular remuneration, proper equipment, medical care, insurance and dependable support for their families. “Welfare, discipline and accountability should develop together,” he said, adding that funding arrangements must be transparent and sustainable enough to cover salaries, training, maintenance, communications, investigations and equipment replacement. He also warned against allowing private interests to dictate police operations, saying security trust funds should only supplement public financing under clear rules and public accountability. “Private contributions must follow clear rules and public accountability; they must never purchase influence over investigations or preferential treatment,” he said. Safeguards against abuse The governor canvassed the use of secure communications, coordinated databases, surveillance and reliable emergency reporting systems to strengthen intelligence gathering and response. He, however, stressed that technology must operate within the law and with safeguards for privacy and accountable access to information. Abiodun said the proposed system must also prevent the police from becoming an instrument of political repression, insisting on independent complaints mechanisms, legislative scrutiny and judicial remedies. He called for the involvement of traditional rulers, religious leaders, women’s organisations, youth groups, farmers, transport workers and other community stakeholders in building an effective intelligence-gathering system. “Fear of criminals must never be compounded by fear of approaching the authorities,” he said. The governor said coordination between federal and state security agencies would be critical, particularly because criminals could exploit jurisdictional boundaries if agencies failed to share intelligence and conduct joint operations. He explained that the proposed architecture was not designed to abolish the Nigeria Police Force but to establish a multi-tier policing system. Under the arrangement, he said, the Federal Police would focus on national security, inter-state crime and counter-terrorism, while State Police would handle intra-state enforcement, community intelligence and crime prevention. “This is not an invitation to disintegration. Our framework incorporates federal oversight, constitutional safeguards, independent State Police Service Commissions, and intelligence-sharing protocols,” Abiodun said. ‘Security reform is economic strategy’ The Ogun governor linked the proposed reform directly to Nigeria’s economic development, arguing that insecurity was no longer merely a law-and-order problem but a threat to investment, food production, infrastructure, livelihoods and national prosperity. “National security today is not just physical protection, it is economic security, food security, health security, financial security and freedom of worship. None survives in lawlessness,” he said. He added: “We cannot build a $1 trillion economy on fragile security. FDI will not flow where investors fear. Agriculture cannot thrive when farmers cannot access farms. Infrastructure cannot yield returns when corridors are unsafe.” “Securing states through State Police is not merely a security strategy; it is our primary economic strategy,” he declared. Aiyedatiwa: Akeredolu’s campaign now national Abiodun credited Akeredolu with helping to move the State Police debate from theory to practical regional action, recalling the late governor’s role in the establishment of the Western Nigeria Security Network, popularly known as Amotekun, in 2020. He said the initiative was created in response to kidnapping, banditry and attacks on farmers and travellers across the Southwest. “When others weighed political expediency, Aketi stepped into the arena,” Abiodun said. He added that Akeredolu understood that “no Governor can be Chief Security Officer in name only, without operational command.” Abiodun said Amotekun demonstrated that local intelligence and regional cooperation could complement the Federal Police and provide faster responses to security threats. He also noted Akeredolu’s support for regional economic development, including the emergence of the Southwest Development Commission. “The greatest tribute is not to praise his past, but to complete his unfinished work,” Abiodun said. He commended President Bola Tinubu for supporting State Police reform through a constitutional framework and urged stakeholders to ensure that the process was concluded. “President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, has shown the courage to champion and lead this conversation. We must now push this reform across the finish line,” he said. In his remarks, Ondo State Governor, Lucky Aiyedatiwa, said Akeredolu’s advocacy for State Police had moved from a regional campaign to the centre of Nigeria’s national policy and constitutional conversation. Aiyedatiwa, who was Akeredolu’s deputy before succeeding him as governor, said the late governor regarded public office as an instrument of service rather than an ornament of status. He described Akeredolu’s career as Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Ondo State, President of the Nigerian Bar Association, governor and Chairman of the Southwest Governors’ Forum as one defined by legal scholarship, courage and commitment to justice. “The establishment of the Southwest Security Network, the Amotekun Corps, represented a bold assertion that those closest to the people must have a meaningful role in protecting them,” Aiyedatiwa said. He said what Akeredolu and other advocates had advanced as a response to the realities of Nigeria’s federal structure had now entered the centre of the country’s national policy debate. “What Akeredolu and other progressive voices once advanced as a necessary response to the realities of our federal structure has now entered the very centre of Nigeria’s national policy and constitutional conversation,” he said. Aiyedatiwa said the challenge was to develop a State Police system that would be responsive, professional and accountable while protecting citizens against abuse. He identified credible recruitment and vetting, professional training, sustainable funding, effective oversight, respect for human rights, clearly defined jurisdictions and safeguards against abuse as essential components of the proposed architecture. DAWN: Debate now about ‘how’ Also speaking, the Director-General of the Development Agenda for Western Nigeria, DAWN, Commission, Dr Seye Oyeleye, said the debate had moved from whether Nigeria should establish State Police to how the system would be implemented. “The debate on state policing is no longer about whether. It is about how. How do we fund it? How do we train and equip it? How do we guard against abuse? How do we keep it accountable to the people, not to politicians?” he said. Oyeleye said the issue was not a regional or ethnic agenda but a national imperative arising from Nigeria’s federal structure and security realities. “This is not a regional agenda. It is not a Yoruba agenda. It is a national agenda. State Policing goes to the heart of our nationhood,” he said. He said the experience of Amotekun had demonstrated the value of regional cooperation and local intelligence in addressing security challenges. “Amotekun showed what is possible. Regional cooperation works. Local knowledge saves lives,” he said. Former Ekiti State Governor, Dr Kayode Fayemi, also paid tribute to Akeredolu, recalling his courage, commitment to justice and advocacy for a decentralised security architecture. Fayemi, who worked closely with Akeredolu during their years in the Southwest Governors’ Forum, said the late governor’s contribution to the debate on multi-level policing had outlived his tenure. The colloquium also featured tributes from Akeredolu’s family, friends and professional associates, as well as panel discussions on the future of State Police and the region’s security architecture. The event was attended by governors, former governors, lawmakers, security chiefs, traditional rulers, academics, civil society actors and other stakeholders.
