title: Venezuela’s ex-leader Nicolás Maduro charged with conspiracy to commit torture
body: Prosecutors in the United States have accused Venezuela’s former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, of conspiracy to commit torture. The fresh charges against the couple were made public on Thursday and are in addition to the drug-trafficking and weapons charges already brought against them, which they have denied. Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, have been in custody since January in a detention centre in Brooklyn, where they were taken after US forces seized them in a pre-dawn raid on their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas. Human rights groups in Venezuela and former prisoners have long denounced what they have described as “systematic torture” in Venezuelan jails. The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027. Both are being held in a detention centre in Brooklyn and are expected to remain there after Flores’s request to be moved to house arrest was denied by a judge on Thursday. The new accusations relate to the alleged torture of US citizens who were being held in Venezuela while Maduro was in power. The superseding indictment unsealed on Thursday accuses the former presidential couple of “entrenching themselves in power” by presiding “over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens”. According to the indictment, the torture included “electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture”. The prosecutors allege that the psychological torture included threats to kill victims’ families, including children. The motivation behind the repression, according to the indictment, was to ensure that Maduro and his wife remained in power. The prosecution accuses Flores of having played a key role in the development of the repressive system, ordering that individuals be tortured and even receiving updates on the torture of specific prisoners. The court document alleges that she did so in order to protect members of her family who were involved in illegal activities. The allegations contained in the superseding indictment echo many of the accusations long made by prisoners who have been released from detention in Venezuela. Javier Tarazona, the head of a human rights group in Venezuela, told BBC Mundo’s Norberto Paredes earlier this year how he and his brother were held in a tiny punishment cell for 46 days after being arbitrarily arrested. Another former inmate, Ángel Godoy, told BBC Mundo that he was kept isolated for months and not allowed to contact his wife, who was in turn kept in the dark about his whereabouts. The allegations listed in the superseding indictment made public on Thursday relate to cases during Maduro’s time in power. After his ouster, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, was sworn in as interim leader with the backing of the Trump administration. While hundreds of political prisoners have been released under an amnesty law since she has taken over power, more than 300 still remain behind bars, according to prisoners’ rights group Foro Penal. The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk has warned that his office has received reports alleging that detainees continue to be tortured even after the seizure of Maduro. Türk said in March that “structural and systemic human rights concerns” had persisted in Venezuela despite Maduro’s ousting.

title: Two 14-year-old boys killed by an explosive device in a field in Sumy Oblast
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Two 14-year-old boys were killed when an explosive device detonated in the evening in the Konotop district of Sumy Oblast, according to the statement by Oleh Hryhorov, head of the Sumy Regional Military Administration. The children encountered the dangerous device in a field, suffered severe injuries, and died at the scene, the statement said. In 2022, Russian forces occupied parts of Sumy Oblast, but Ukraine liberated the region in April. Russia intensified its offensive again in 2025. Today, mines, unexploded ordnance and Russian drones shot down over the region pose a danger, as their warheads can detonate after falling. Overall, 146 children in Ukraine have suffered mine-related injuries, former Interior Minister Ihor Klymenko reported in April. For example, two months ago, an 11-year-old boy and a 15-year-old boy in Sumy Oblast were injured when an explosive device detonated. Hryhorov expressed his condolences to the parents and relatives of the victims and urged people to remain cautious: “Please be as careful as possible and remind children: do not approach unknown or suspicious objects, touch them, or try to move them. Take care of yourselves and your loved ones,” Hryhorov said. Demining efforts continue in Sumy Oblast On 24 February 2022, Russian forces entered the territory of Sumy Oblast. The first battles in the region took place that same day. In particular, Russian forces attempted to break through to Sumy, but Ukrainian troops repelled the offensive. On 11 April 2022, Ukraine restored control over the entire Sumy region. As early as 7 June 2022, deminers were working in the Konotop, Sumy, and Okhtyrka districts, according to the Government Portal. That day, they surveyed areas and neutralized explosive devices. The work of deminers remains deadly dangerous. In September 2024, two pyrotechnicians from Dnipropetrovsk Oblast were hit by a mine while demining Sumy Oblast: one died, while the other was hospitalized. In July 2025, deminer Oleh Petrenko was killed during humanitarian demining operations in Shostka District when a Russian FPV drone detonated, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine reported . Another pyrotechnician was injured, the statement said. Nevertheless, the work continues despite the danger. In 2025, State Emergency Service deminers in the Sumy Oblast found and neutralized 5,283 explosive devices, the agency said in April. Sumy Oblast ranked sixth among all Ukrainian regions by this figure. Twenty-two percent of Ukraine’s territory is potentially contaminated with explosive devices — more than 133,000 square kilometers, former Interior Minister Ihor Klymenko reported in April this year. Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, State Emergency Service and National Police deminers have surveyed more than 248,000 hectares of territory and found more than 1 million 112 thousand explosive devices, the statement said. title: US Air Force, Army eye industry access on test ranges
body: Earlier this year, the Army announced it was opening five of its military test ranges – four domestic and one overseas – to approved companies in a move designed to speed innovation and get weapons and tech to the warfighter faster. Now, the Air Force says it’s considering a similar move. In a forum hosted by the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies on Tuesday, the commander of the Air Force Test Center, Brig. Gen. Mark Massaro, said service leaders were “actively working with the Army” to understand how they could apply the concept. “We’re … looking at how the Army has opened up some of their ranges to commercial access and understanding what it is that we can do, on the Air Force side, to maybe move forward in that direction,” Massaro said. The Air Force, he said, has had discussions with leaders from Army Test and Evaluation Command to “understand where they have gone with their access to ranges … to open up opportunities for contractors,” he said. He added that in a previous posting as commander of the 96th Test Wing at Eglin Air Force Base, Fla., he had worked with Air Force officials and contractors to arrange smaller-scale test range access for specific tests. That experience, he said, had yielded “a lot of lessons” for how the arrangement could work. He acknowledged the threat from adversaries gathering imagery from above – an existing and growing risk with the rise of drone incursions that such a move might exacerbate. “We do understand that we have critical capabilities that we’re testing and we need to protect them,” Massaro said. “We do understand that there is a threat from an information security standpoint that we do pay attention to when we execute our tests, and we do work to design our processes and our ways of testing to account for that.” But the advantages, he said, are also evident. “Industry really is leading the way in a lot of ways on exploration and development, using their own internal research and development,” Massaro said. “And allowing them the ability to gain access to capabilities like the ranges helps … them to accelerate that learning to a point when it may become a useful, relevant technology for our military to consider using … So to to help them along that process in ways that we can through range or other assets, enable some of that work to help move the needle forward.” Former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll made the opening of service test ranges to industry one of the centerpieces of his work to eliminate barriers to industry and drive efficiency in innovation. In a January interview with CBS, he described conditions that private companies couldn’t easily replicate on their own, such as a range set up to imitate a Ukrainian battlefield and space to test anti-jamming and hypersonic weapons technology. He also said that opening Army ranges would cut down the traditional range test process from up to 18 months to as little as 30 days. “A company with a good idea shouldn’t need a team of lawyers and a program of record just to prove their equipment works,” Driscoll said in an August statement announcing the range openings. “So we fixed that. One front door … a real person to walk you in, and on the other side, everything the modern battlefield demands: contested airspace, degraded signals and the space to test at real scale.” The ranges the Army made available to industry via an online application portal include Dugway Proving Ground, Utah; West Cibola Range, part of Yuma Proving Ground, Ariz.; Camp Shelby Joint Forces Training Center, Miss.; Camp Grayling Joint Maneuver Training Center, Mich.; and the Multidomain Training Area range complex within the Morocco-based Africa Multidomain Training and Experimentation Center.

title: US Air Force, Army eye industry access on test ranges
body: Earlier this year, the Army announced it was opening five of its military test ranges – four domestic and one overseas – to approved companies in a move designed to speed innovation and get weapons and tech to the warfighter faster. Now, the Air Force says it’s considering a similar move. In a forum hosted by the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies on Tuesday, the commander of the Air Force Test Center, Brig. Gen. Mark Massaro, said service leaders were “actively working with the Army” to understand how they could apply the concept. “We’re … looking at how the Army has opened up some of their ranges to commercial access and understanding what it is that we can do, on the Air Force side, to maybe move forward in that direction,” Massaro said. The Air Force, he said, has had discussions with leaders from Army Test and Evaluation Command to “understand where they have gone with their access to ranges … to open up opportunities for contractors,” he said. He added that in a previous posting as commander of the 96th Test Wing at Eglin Air Force Base, Fla., he had worked with Air Force officials and contractors to arrange smaller-scale test range access for specific tests. That experience, he said, had yielded “a lot of lessons” for how the arrangement could work. He acknowledged the threat from adversaries gathering imagery from above – an existing and growing risk with the rise of drone incursions that such a move might exacerbate. “We do understand that we have critical capabilities that we’re testing and we need to protect them,” Massaro said. “We do understand that there is a threat from an information security standpoint that we do pay attention to when we execute our tests, and we do work to design our processes and our ways of testing to account for that.” But the advantages, he said, are also evident. “Industry really is leading the way in a lot of ways on exploration and development, using their own internal research and development,” Massaro said. “And allowing them the ability to gain access to capabilities like the ranges helps … them to accelerate that learning to a point when it may become a useful, relevant technology for our military to consider using … So to to help them along that process in ways that we can through range or other assets, enable some of that work to help move the needle forward.” Former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll made the opening of service test ranges to industry one of the centerpieces of his work to eliminate barriers to industry and drive efficiency in innovation. In a January interview with CBS, he described conditions that private companies couldn’t easily replicate on their own, such as a range set up to imitate a Ukrainian battlefield and space to test anti-jamming and hypersonic weapons technology. He also said that opening Army ranges would cut down the traditional range test process from up to 18 months to as little as 30 days. “A company with a good idea shouldn’t need a team of lawyers and a program of record just to prove their equipment works,” Driscoll said in an August statement announcing the range openings. “So we fixed that. title: C’River shuts 9 more schools over lack of operating approval
body: By Ike Uchechukwu, CALABAR The Cross River State Government has sealed nine schools in Calabar Municipality for operating without the required Approval to Operate (ATO), extending its clampdown on unregistered institutions. The Quality Assurance Department of the Ministry of Education carried out the exercise. It follows the closure of about 24 schools in Calabar South and reflects the government’s drive to ensure that schools across the state meet approved regulatory and operational standards. The government said the exercise was aimed at protecting the quality of education and ensuring that learners are taught in safe, conducive and suitable environments. It also seeks to bring school proprietors into compliance with the requirements for operating educational institutions in the state. Speaking on the enforcement, the Commissioner for Education, Prof. Stephen Odey, said the government would not compromise the standards required for schools to operate legally in Cross River. Odey explained that the inspections were designed to identify schools operating outside the approved regulatory framework and compel proprietors to obtain the necessary approvals and meet prescribed standards. He warned proprietors of the sealed schools against reopening without government authorisation, stressing that any attempt to violate the directive would attract appropriate sanctions. The commissioner said the regulatory checks would continue across the 18 Local Government Areas of the state. He noted that schools found operating without approval would be given the opportunity to regularise their operations in line with established requirements. The Ministry of Education urged proprietors across the state to obtain the necessary approval and maintain continuous compliance with the prescribed standards. The government said the exercise would continue as part of efforts to strengthen regulation of the education sector, protect learners and uphold the integrity and quality of education in Cross River State. The post C’River shuts 9 more schools over lack of operating approval appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: UN Security Council extends arms embargo in Sudan's Darfur as US pushes for nationwide ban
body: The UN Security Council unanimously voted on Thursday to extend an arms embargo on Sudan ’s Darfur region until December 11, buying time for negotiations over a US proposal to widen the restrictions to the entire country. The short extension highlighted disagreements over how to stop weapons from reaching those fighting in Sudan’s civil war, now in its fourth year. Washington has pushed for a nationwide embargo, while China, Russia and other council members want to keep the sanctions confined to Darfur. Although the embargo has failed to stop weapons reaching Darfur, it allows UN experts to investigate arms shipments and identify those responsible for breaches, paving the way for any further sanctions. Massad Boulos , US senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, proposed expanding the embargo in August. Working with Mike Waltz, Washington’s ambassador to the UN, he sought to increase pressure on the warring Sudanese Armed Forces and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. “The United States has presented a resolution to the Security Council that would expand the arms embargo nationwide, making clear that sanctions and member state implementation of those rules apply to all the networks keeping this war alive on both sides, with no carve-outs,” Mr Boulos and Mr Waltz wrote in an opinion piece for Foreign Policy in September. The two said that nationwide restrictions would take aim at arms traffickers, financiers, mercenary recruiters and drone suppliers. But the proposal met resistance from China and Russia, which hold veto power, as well as the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Liberia, Somalia and Pakistan. Tension between Washington and Khartoum increased after the US reportedly withheld a visa for Gen Abdel Fattah Al Burhan, head of the Sudanese Armed Forces, before his scheduled UN General Assembly address last month. Reuters reported that the decision appeared to be linked to his resistance to a US-backed ceasefire plan. Sudan has claimed it did not reject the US ceasefire proposal but instead submitted comments on it. US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said last month that neither the SAF nor the RSF represented a legitimate constitutional government for Sudan.

title: Eight soldiers reported dead as troops foil terror attack in Borno
body:
At least eight soldiers have reportedly been killed while repelling an attack by Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) terrorists on a military base in Kukawa Local Government Area of Borno State.
The attack targeted troops of the 101 Special Forces Battalion, who came under assault from four different directions, according to a statement by Operation Hadin Kai, a joint task force in the North-east.
The troops, supported by the Nigerian Air Force, responded with superior firepower and tactical manoeuvres, killing more than 25 terrorists and forcing others to flee, the task force’s spokesperson, Mohammed Goni said.
Mr Goni, a Nigerian Army captain, said 14 bodies of the terrorists had so far been recovered, while troops also seized a cache of weapons and ammunition, including six AK-47 rifles.
However, the military spokesperson acknowledged that some soldiers were killed during the fierce encounter, although it did not disclose the exact number of casualties.
SaharaReporters reported that eight soldiers were killed in the attack, citing military sources.
Mr Goni said troops were continuing to exploit the area to recover additional weapons, track fleeing terrorists and prevent them from regrouping.
The attack comes as security forces continue intensified operations against ISWAP and Boko Haram insurgents in the North-east, where military formations and civilian communities have remained targets of terrorist attacks.
Mr Goni said the military commiserated with the families of the soldiers who died in the encounter.
“Their courage, sacrifice and devotion to duty will remain an enduring testament to their service to the nation,” he said.
The military spokesperson described the successful repulsion of the attack as evidence of the combat readiness of troops and improved coordination between ground forces and the Air Component.
He said troops would sustain aggressive patrols, intelligence-led operations and coordinated offensive actions with other security agencies to dismantle terrorist networks and protect communities.

title: Second mass stabbing attack carried out, filmed in Poland in 'grim copycat phenomenon'
body: A 15-year-old former pupil killed one employee and injured two others at a Polish primary school on Thursday while wearing a helmet-mounted camera, the second school stabbing in two days, possibly in response to an internet challenge, authorities said.A 37-year-old woman who worked as a caretaker had died in the latest attack, which took place at around 9 a.m. in Leszczydol-Nowiny, northeast of Warsaw, officials said.On Wednesday, a 19-year-old wounded 10 people, including himself, at another school in Ostroleka, northeastern Poland, and police detained a 17-year-old in Sierpc in north-central Poland on suspicion of planning an attack."We fear a grim copycat phenomenon," Prime Minister Donald Tusk told an emergency meeting."We are facing an extraordinary situation... for the first time, we are dealing with a killer who wore a helmet-mounted camera, intending to film the knife attack." It was not clear whether the attack was actually filmed.Teachers injured restraining attackerHe ordered police to visit schools daily in an effort to prevent further violence.A police spokesperson said authorities had information that the incidents could be related to an internet challenge and that this was being investigated.Tusk praised the heroism of two teachers at the school who were injured as they tried to stop the attacker.Head teacher Krzysztof Ochmanski said he had heard a scream and ran into the corridor."He wounded me with the blade of a rather long knife - he had three knives on him - and hit me with the handle," he told the public broadcaster Polskie Radio RDC. "By then, I had managed to restrain him."A Reuters reporter saw an air ambulance flying away from the school, where a small crowd had gathered. The father of one child, waiting outside the school, said pupils had not yet been allowed to leave, but were safe.Serious offenders becoming younger across EuropeFootage on public news broadcaster TVP Info showed what appeared to be the attacker being handcuffed and put into a police van.Inspector Katarzyna Nowak, director of communications for the national police, said serious offenders were becoming younger across Europe."Over the past few months in Poland, we have seen arrests of teenagers who were preparing to carry out attacks... So, this is indeed a problem we face, and one we must acknowledge," she told TVP Info.Interior minister Marcin Kierwinski said that the 17-year-old detained in Sierpc had mentioned plans to do "something dangerous" on school grounds."Data recovered from electronic devices revealed online searches regarding how to orchestrate such a violent event," Kierwinski said. Police found two knives in his possession.

title: University of Guelph, police to join ‘homecoming working group’ after chaotic party
body:
Police in Guelph say they’re establishing a “homecoming working group” to manage large unsanctioned gatherings after a chaotic University of Guelph party made headlines last week.
Police say the working group is being jointly created with the city, the University of Guelph and Guelph General Hospital to support community safety and identify ways to hold offenders accountable.
The force says police, the hospital and municipal services already do extensive planning each year in the run-up to homecoming, but “this year demonstrated that the environment surrounding unsanctioned gatherings has changed.”
Videos from an off-campus homecoming party on Sept. 26 showed massive crowds of young people in the streets, with some throwing bottles and other objects as police officers tried to control the situation.
Guelph police said at the time the gathering was “significantly larger” than similar events in recent years and officers were dealing with people climbing buildings, as well as shoplifting and vandalism at nearby businesses.
University of Guelph president Rene Van Acker said last week the party risked the safety of students and neighbours and the university was reviewing the incident.
Police say social media and “individuals who encourage disorder” have played key roles in escalating the size and risks of unsanctioned gatherings.
They say the working group will meet regularly to consider recommendations on how to prevent and respond to gatherings of this kind.
Last week, police asked for the public’s help identifying people seen in social media videos of the Sept. 26 party.
The force said several people were charged with criminal and provincial offences over that weekend.

title: Nestlé Ghana expansion shows Ghana’s 24-hour economy in action – Mahama
body: President John Dramani Mahama has described the expansion of Nestlé Ghana’s Tema factory as a clear demonstration of the government’s 24-hour economy in action, saying the investment reflects Ghana’s ambition to produce more of what it consumes and export more of what it produces. He said the expansion represents the kind of industrial investment needed to strengthen local production, create jobs and increase value addition within the Ghanaian economy. President Mahama was speaking on Thursday, October 8, 2026, when he commissioned Nestlé Ghana Limited’s expanded evaporated milk production line at its Tema factory. The new production line replaces one that had served the factory for more than 30 years and is expected to significantly increase the company’s production capacity. According to the President, annual production capacity will rise from approximately 12,960 tonnes to nearly 30,000 tonnes following the expansion. He said the upgraded facility would enable Nestlé to undertake the filling, homogenisation, sterilisation and packaging of milk locally, using Ghanaian workers. President Mahama said developments of this nature were critical to his administration’s efforts to transform Ghana from an economy heavily dependent on imports into one with stronger domestic production and export capacity. He has previously linked the expansion of industrial activity in Tema to the government’s broader economic agenda, noting that the industrial enclave is gradually regaining its position as a major manufacturing hub. The Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Elizabeth Ofosu-Adjare, said the growing investment activity in Ghana was evidence of increased interest in the country’s economic prospects. She disclosed that Ghana’s Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) inflows increased from US$652 million in 2024 to US$2.62 billion in 2025. The latest investment data also show that manufacturing recorded the highest number of investment projects in 2025, with 99 projects, ahead of mining, oil and gas, and general trade. Madam Ofosu-Adjare said the figures demonstrate that investors are responding positively to the government’s call for Ghana to become a more attractive destination for business and investment. The Nestlé expansion forms part of a wider pattern of industrial investments in the Tema enclave, which President Mahama says is beginning to reclaim its former industrial prominence. The President has stressed that the ultimate objective is to build an economy where investments translate into increased production, jobs, stronger local businesses and greater access to regional and international markets.

title: Sybiha calls on Russia to disclose all information about possible plague outbreak
body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha, commenting on reports of a possible plague outbreak in Irkutsk, called on Russia to disclose all information regarding the incident.
"What is Russia hiding in Irkutsk? On October 2, 28-year-old Daria Shipilova died at Shelekhov District Hospital. She worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Soon after her death, reports began circulating in the Irkutsk region that she had died of pneumonic plague," the minister said on X.
He said that nearly 200 people who had been in contact with Shipilova were isolated and placed under medical observation, and quarantine measures were implemented in several hospitals in Irkutsk.
Sybiha said Russia has a long history of concealing the truth: the 1979 anthrax leak in Sverdlovsk; the 1986 Chornobyl disaster; the true scale of COVID-19 in 2020-2022.
"Each time, the consequences were devastating. There is credible evidence that Russia has used chemical weapons in Ukraine. It also threatens to use nuclear weapons in its genocidal war. The world must not wait for another catastrophe before asking questions," the foreign minister said.
He said Russia must disclose all the circumstances of this case, provide transparent epidemiological data, and cooperate with international mechanisms.
"When dangerous pathogens are involved, secrecy is a threat to everyone," the statement reads.
On October 6, the Public Health Center of the Ukrainian Ministry of Health said it is monitoring reports of a suspected particularly dangerous infection in Irkutsk region and currently considers the risk to Ukraine to be very low.
Plague is an acute bacterial infection caused by Yersinia pestis. The natural reservoir of the pathogen is primarily small mammals, and transmission to humans can occur through bites from infected fleas, direct contact with infected tissues or materials, or – in the case of the pneumonic form – through infected respiratory droplets.

title: Portugal puts F-35 back under serious consideration after 2025 doubts
body:
Portugal is seriously considering the Lockheed Martin F-35A as a replacement for its F-16 fighters , Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel said on Thursday. His statement signals a change from the doubts raised by the government over the US aircraft last year.
“We are seriously considering the F-35 proposal, just as we are considering others,” Rangel said after a meeting in Lisbon with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. He added that Portugal would make its decision according to the country's national interest.
Portugal has not formally selected a successor to its F-16M fleet. The competition also includes the Saab Gripen E, Dassault Rafale and Eurofighter Typhoon , with their manufacturers pursuing a program that could cover between 14 and 28 fighters.
The F-35's position appeared less certain in March 2025, when Defense Minister Nuno Melo questioned whether Portugal should remain dependent on the United States for a future fighter fleet. His concerns centered on the political relationship with Washington under President Donald Trump and the long-term dependence on US support, components and software.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
The Portuguese Air Force maintained a different position. Its chief of staff, Gen. João Cartaxo Alves, publicly argued that Portugal needed a fifth-generation fighter and identified the F-35 as the available aircraft that met that requirement.
An internal Portuguese Air Force assessment subsequently placed the F-35 ahead of its European competitors. The study compared the candidates under 20 criteria, with the Gripen E reportedly in second place. The assessment represents a military recommendation rather than a government selection.
The potential acquisition has been estimated at between €3 billion and €5 billion (approximately US$3.5 billion to US$5.8 billion), depending on the number of aircraft and configuration of the program. Portugal currently operates 28 upgraded F-16s, although a future order could involve fewer fighters.
Lockheed Martin has also sought to address the industrial side of the competition. The US manufacturer has discussed F-35 component production and maintenance activities in Portugal and identified potential projects involving Portuguese companies.
European manufacturers continue to pursue the requirement. Dassault has presented the Rafale to Portugal, Saab is promoting the Gripen E and Airbus is preparing a Eurofighter proposal that includes financing and industrial participation.
The political debate over dependence on the United States has not disappeared. Former Defense Minister João Gomes Cravinho said in September that purchasing the F-35 would leave Portugal dependent on Washington for decades, although he acknowledged the fighter's capabilities.
Rubio's visit nevertheless provides a different political setting from early 2025. Portuguese media reported before Thursday's meeting that the F-35 would be among the subjects discussed in Lisbon. The United States and Portugal also maintain a longstanding defense relationship that includes US military access to Lajes Field in the Azores.
Portugal has not announced a timetable for selecting its next fighter or the final number of aircraft it intends to acquire.

title: FG Targets ₦1,350/Litre Ceiling On Petrol Cost To Stabilise Pump Prices
body: The Federal Government says it is targeting a ₦1,350-per-litre ceiling on the ex-gantry or landing cost of petrol as part of measures to cushion the impact of high fuel prices on Nigerians and stabilise pump prices. The Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, disclosed this on Thursday at a briefing on fuel prices and subsidy questions in Abuja. Oyedele said the government was taking further steps because existing measures had not fully addressed the pressure on households and businesses following increases in fuel and transportation costs. Under the proposed price modulation mechanism, the government is negotiating a ₦1,350-per-litre ceiling on the ex-gantry or landing cost of petrol, subject to monthly reviews. The proposed ceiling does not mean petrol will sell for ₦1,350 per litre at filling stations but is rather intended to prevent sharp movements in global crude prices or the exchange rate from immediately translating into corresponding increases in the cost of petrol. “Pump prices should not have to follow every swing in global crude or the exchange rate. The government is negotiating a ceiling of ₦1,350 a litre on the ex-gantry or landing cost of petrol to keep pump prices stable,” Oyedele said. He added that where the cost rises above the ceiling, refiners and importers would initially bear the shortfall and recover it later when market conditions allow. Oyedele said the arrangement was neither a subsidy nor price control, but a mechanism designed to smooth out petrol prices over time. “The reasoning is simple: ₦1,400 a litre today and ₦1,400 a litre tomorrow is better than ₦1,500 a litre today and ₦1,300 a litre tomorrow,” he said. “Why? Because volatility itself adds to uncertainty and cost, and when fuel goes up sharply, they rarely come down as fast.” He said the ceiling would be reviewed monthly, with the figures published for transparency. As part of the wider measures, the government also plans to offer a temporary margin discount on petrol dispensed by the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited for an initial 30 days, with priority given to public transporters nationwide. The minister stressed that the discount was not a return to fuel subsidy, but an arrangement to sell the product at cost. The government is also exploring forward sales of crude oil to local refiners as domestic production increases, allowing committed crude supplies to be freed up and helping shield pump prices from global market swings. Other measures include working with state authorities to eliminate illegal levies and road-use charges that add to transportation costs, increasing funding for cash transfers to vulnerable households and providing more direct credit support for small businesses. The government also plans to accelerate the rollout of compressed natural gas for transport operators, with the expectation that operators would pass the resulting savings on to commuters. Oyedele said sanctions could be applied against operators who exploit consumers, while proceeds from enforcement actions would be channelled into transport support. The government is also considering an excess profits tax and targeted vouchers for low-income earners, alongside measures to reduce regulatory costs and red tape that drive up the prices of goods and services. It further plans to establish a national strategic fuel reserve to strengthen supply security and guard against disruptions or hoarding, while improving traffic management and logistics to reduce fuel consumption. Oyedele said the government would also leverage NIPOST address codes to help lower logistics costs. He said the measures would be scaled up in collaboration with state governments, stressing that the objective was to ensure assistance reaches those who need it most without creating additional pressure on the wider economy. The post FG Targets ₦1,350/Litre Ceiling On Petrol Cost To Stabilise Pump Prices appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Ukraine open to restoring dialogue with South Korea despite Seoul’s decision to recall ambassador – MFA
body:
MFA spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said this to journalists, according to Ukrinform.
According to Tykhyi, this week the ministry invited the Republic of Korea’s ambassador to Ukraine to present the Ukrainian position and seek constructive solutions.
“We conveyed the Ukrainian side’s position to him. We are convinced that diplomacy should prevail over emotions. Despite Seoul’s decision to recall its ambassador, Ukraine remains open to restoring constructive dialogue – even if it takes time,” the diplomat said.
As reported by Ukrinform, the South Korean government decided to recall its ambassador in Kyiv over differences regarding the situation involving prisoners of war from North Korea.
Earlier, the South Korean presidential office expressed “deep regret” over what Seoul said was Ukraine’s denial of an agreement not to disclose information about the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
Presidential Communications Adviser Dmytro Lytvyn wrote on Facebook that there had been no non-disclosure agreement and that it would be wrong to conceal where the prisoners were being transferred. In response to a request from Yonhap, the Presidential Office explained that Kyiv had disclosed only the fact of the transfer without revealing details of the process.
South Korea later received an apology from Ukraine for disclosing information about the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul. However, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said the apology did not meet the government’s expectations.

title: Prince Harry reveals he ‘slipped into depression’ after moving to Canada
body:
Prince Harry is opening about about his move to Canada in late 2019 and the toll it took on his mental health.
In a new MasterClass , which is a streaming platform for online learning, the Duke of Sussex said he experienced an “adrenaline crash” after relocating from England to Vancouver Island in 2019.
“It was myself, my wife and our son Archie, and we moved to Canada to get some space away from everything just to be able to think,” Harry said, according to People and The Hollywood Reporter .
“Being in Canada, away from the stressful environment where presumably my body was just pumped full of adrenaline, within two or three days, I experienced this adrenaline crash, something that I’d never experienced before,” Harry continued.
“It was as if I needed stress in order to get the adrenaline to make my brain function because I became useless around the house,” he added.
Harry revealed that he started to struggle with his mental health following the move.
“I actually slipped into depression for about two weeks. I felt like I couldn’t function without the adrenaline,” he revealed.
Harry spoke about the move to Canada in the MasterClass titled, Redefining Grief: Building Resilience Through Loss, while speaking with neuroscientist Dr. Mary-Frances O’Connor.
During the MasterClass, Harry also spoke about the grief he experienced after losing his mother, the late Princess Diana , at the age of 12.
“I couldn’t remember my mom’s laugh. I couldn’t remember what she looked like. I felt like I had to be sad in order to prove to her that I miss her,” Harry said .
“In my 20s, I went to war twice thinking I could outrun my feelings. But that’s not what happened,” he added. “I’d spent so long emotionally numb to a large extent because nobody told me joy was still allowed. That it wasn’t betrayal.”
Harry and his wife, Meghan Markle , moved to Canada in late 2019 with their son Prince Archie. In January 2020, the couple announced that they were stepping down as working senior members of the British Royal Family .
When the couple first moved to Canada they announced that they’d be financially supporting themselves, living primarily in Canada and paying back British taxpayers for the multi-million dollar renovations on their Windsor home of Frogmore Cottage.
The family of three spent six weeks in Victoria over the Christmas holidays in 2019, which first prompted speculation that they’d be purchasing a home in the Canadian city.
In February 2020, it was revealed that Canadian taxpayers had been paying some of the security costs for Harry and Meghan since November 2019 but that would stop “in the coming weeks,” a spokesperson for then-public safety minister Bill Blair told Global News at the time.
“The Duke and Duchess of Sussex choosing to re-locate to Canada on a part-time basis presented our government with a unique and unprecedented set of circumstances,” the spokesperson said at the time.
“The RCMP has been engaged with officials in the U.K. from the very beginning regarding security considerations. As the Duke and Duchess are currently recognized as Internationally Protected Persons, Canada has an obligation to provide security assistance on an as-needed basis.
“At the request of the Metropolitan Police, the RCMP has been providing assistance to the Met since the arrival of the Duke and Duchess to Canada intermittently since October 2019. The assistance will cease in the coming weeks, in keeping with their change in status.”
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex moved to Montecito, Calif., four months after relocating to Canada.
In June 2020 following the couple’s move to California, the Canadian Taxpayers Federation said the RCMP spent more than $50,000 on overtime and logistics costs to provide security for Harry and Meghan during their stay in B.C.
Documents obtained through an access to information request revealed the total price tag added up to $56,384 for their stay from Nov. 18, 2019, and Jan. 19, 2020. The figure did not include salaries or any overtime costs after Jan. 19.
Harry and Meghan have now returned to Britain , six years after they quit royal duties and relocated to Canada and the U.S.
The couple plans to maintain their home in Montecito, Calif., and their vacation property in Portugal during their return to the United Kingdom for an extended stay, which began this fall, The Associated Press reports.
The location of their new home and details of the children’s school have been kept private but last month, a spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex confirmed the children were changing schools after just two days due to security concerns .
“The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family’s security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements,” a spokesman for Harry and Meghan said in a statement to Reuters.
“The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family,” the spokesperson added.
Reuters reports that the distance between their home and the original school caused concern for their security team due to heavy traffic in the area.

title: Nigerian govt to set up funding agency to boost research, innovation
body:
The federal government had begun efforts to set up a National Research and Innovation Development Fund to boost research and scientific innovation in the country.
Nigeria’s Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Kingsley Udeh, disclosed this on Tuesday when he appeared as a guest on TVC News’ Beyond the Headlines.
Mr Udeh, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria, said the funding agency would be responsible for provision of sustainable financing for research and innovation in Nigeria.
The minister explained that the decision to establish the agency followed findings that Nigeria has abundant research and scientific innovations but lacks the funding needed to translate them into practical applications.
“So we understood that it would require some consensus effort, intentionality, to take these research outcomes from the shelves, from the files, into supporting them to the market, to make revenue for the researchers, for the innovators, and of course, add value to our economy, boost our GDP,” he said.
Mr Udeh said the Federal Executive Council had approved the establishment of the funding agency and that a bill had been forwarded to the National Assembly to secure legislative backing.
He said, upon securing legislative approval, the National Assembly would make an Act to establish the funding agency.
The minister said funding would come from multiple sources, such as government allocations and contributions by companies under provisions of the Tax Act that recognise spending on research and development.
“Now, of course, this fund would be governed by a council made up of not just government people, but innovators themselves, researchers, and it’s guided by global standards,” he remarked.
He acknowledged that the exact amount to be available could not be determined at the moment because the proposed funding mechanism would be calculated as percentages on a year-by-year basis.
“But what I can say is that it’s going to be significant,” he said.
Mr Udeh also said the proposed fund would not be completely under the control of the government.
He explained that its governing council would include researchers, innovators, private-sector representatives and other stakeholders in the science, technology and innovation ecosystem.
“So, this fund wouldn’t just be a government thing because the private sector players that will be putting out their taxable income that are devoted to R&D (Research and Innovative Development) would have their eyes on it,” he said.
According to him, the framework would also align Nigeria with the Science Granting Councils Initiative of Africa.
The minister said the objective was to ensure that research funding reaches projects capable of progressing from prototype to commercialisation.
He also said the government was working to establish an Innovation Hub and Innovation Grid that would serve as a national database of research, inventions and innovations across different sectors.
Mr Udeh said an agreement for the project was currently undergoing screening by the Office of the Attorney-General of the Federation.
He said the proposed Innovation Grid would allow investors and industry players to identify research outcomes and intellectual property available in Nigeria and connect with the universities or research institutions responsible for developing them.
The minister said the project was expected to generate about $10 billion (about N13.6 trillion) annually for Nigeria, while its financing would come from outside government because investors would generate returns from the project.
“This is a project that will pay itself. The investors will make money out of this project,” he said.

title: Powerful nuclear arsenal serves as Russia's main safeguard — Kurchatov Center’s chief
body:
MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Russia’s nuclear arsenal is among the most powerful in the world and serves as the country’s "main safeguard," Mikhail Kovalchuk, President of the Kurchatov Institute National Research Center, said.
"We are alive today only because we possess one of the world’s best and most powerful nuclear arsenals. It is our primary 'safeguard,'" he said in an interview with Dmitry Simes, editor-in-chief of Politika magazine.
Kovalchuk noted that the "nuclear umbrella" is fraying. Whereas there were previously only two nuclear powers – the Soviet Union and the United States – around a dozen countries now possess nuclear weapons.
"Everyone else realizes that they, too, need nuclear weapons to preserve their sovereignty. Despite the IAEA and the non-proliferation regime, nuclear weapons have become – I would say – accessible to the masses. Furthermore, their role as a deterrent will diminish, partly because current generations were born after World War II. For them, the horrors of war are merely images on a TV screen or scenes from a computer game," he added.

title: Consultants for Hydro-Québec defend proposal to double energy costs for data centres
body:
Two consultants hired by Hydro-Québec say they expect the demand from data centres to more than double between 2024 and 2030
The analysts from energy and climate consulting firm Dunsky delivered this message at a public hearing reviewing Hydro-Québec’s proposal to hike rates charged to data centres.
Quebec’s energy regulator, the Régie de l’énergie, is reviewing the potential rate hike.
Hydro-Québec gave Dunsky a mandate to analyze how different North American jurisdictions have reacted to the surge in energy demand from data centres.
Alexis Renaud-Bezot, one of the analysts, said energy consumption from data centres in North America could increase by 133 per cent between 2024 and 2030.
He said other jurisdictions increased rates for data centres to minimize the impact on residential customers.
The proposed Hydro-Québec changes would increase rates for data centres to an average of 13 cents per kilowatt hour, which the utility says is around twice as much as what data centres currently pay as large‑power customers.

title: UK must remain in Jerusalem 'at all costs', says former diplomat
body: The UK should keep a diplomatic presence in Jerusalem at all costs to prevent Israeli claims to the disputed city, a former British diplomat has said. Sir Vincent Fean, who served as British Consul General in Jerusalem , said the UK’s historic presence in Jerusalem was critical to maintaining British policy that views the city as a shared capital. It has held a mission in the city for 200 years. He spoke to The National after Israel announced the closure of the Consulate General in Jerusalem, with UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband responding that the building would remain open as a mission. Israel used different wording, saying the building would house a British government-operated task force. “Their scope of activity will be very limited,” Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said. The downgrade in status follows a dispute over British trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Avoiding full closure of the consulate allows the two allies to continue talks and minimises the risk of a permanent rupture amid intense domestic debate over the relationship in both countries. In recent days, there have been suggestions Britain was prepared ⁠to consider ejecting Israeli diplomats if the mission were ‌closed. “It will be known as the UK mission. It doesn’t really matter. What matters is that the mission is in Jerusalem,” Mr Fean told The National. “If it's not there it will be very hard to get it back. One of the Israeli aims is to ensure any future embassy is in Ramallah [in the West Bank]. British officials could be seen leaving the building on Thursday, as all but seven staff members were made to move by the Israeli government to the embassy in Tel Aviv. Workers removed ​signs ​and plaques from the walls overnight. The decision came after weeks of negotiations, which may have continued until late on Wednesday when the Israeli decision was announced. Mr Saar acknowledged the building was UK property, which prevented the Israeli government from seizing control of it and expelling all the diplomats. The UK first established a Consulate General in 1838, 110 years before the state of Israel was declared, and has been operating from the building in Sheikh Jarrah in East Jerusalem since 1965. It is thought Mr Miliband could be buying time until after the Israel elections at the end of this month, before resuming talks with what could potentially be a new government, Mr Fean said. “There is a time factor, which is October 27 and the Israeli elections. That could mean a different set of interlocutors,” he added. Both Downing Street and the Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) were involved in the negotiations leading up to Thursday, with UK National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell visiting Jerusalem last week. The Israeli decision was “unlawful and disproportionate”, Mr Fean said. “Israel is taking it out in essence on Palestinians and British nationals, rather than on bilateral relations between Israeli and the UK.” Concerns have been raised about the implications for consular services for British citizens and Palestinians, but the visa service is expected to remain “intact”, with an office in Ramallah that does not have diplomatic status, Mr Fean said. But some British charities have raised concerns over the potential impact on their ability to deliver aid in the Palestinian territories. “The British Consulate General is a lifeline,” said Aseel Baidoun of Medical Aid for Palestinians. “It is the UK's main channel to Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza. “It is essential for enabling close co-ordination with humanitarian and health organisations working there, including Medical Aid for Palestinians. Downgrading the Consulate General will reduce the UK's ability to protect Palestinian civilians, support aid delivery and uphold international law at the very moment these are most needed,” she told The National. “Israel's closure order was retaliation for the UK taking lawful action against illegal settlements. The UK should make clear that it will not reward attempts to entrench Israel's annexation of East Jerusalem.” Last week, Dominic Grieve KC, who was the government’s senior legal adviser from 2010 to 2014, said the closure was “an unlawful assertion of Israeli sovereignty over occupied East Jerusalem ”. He wrote to the FCDO to argue Israel was furthering its agenda to annex East Jerusalem by closing the British consulate.

title: Supreme Court Judgement: Parties that violate membership register rule won’t field candidates – INEC
body:
The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has said political parties that violated the statutory requirement on membership registers will not be allowed to field candidates in the 2027 general elections.
INEC National Commissioner for Information and Voter Education, Mohammed Haruna, disclosed this on Wednesday when he appeared on Trust TV’s Daily Politics programme.
Mr Haruna said the commission would not allow parties to substitute candidates affected by the Supreme Court’s recent judgment on the submission and use of party membership registers.
He said allowing such parties to substitute the affected candidates would amount to making them to benefit from their own violation of the law.
“It’s like you committed an offence and then, you come and benefit from it. You remember cases that we had of some in Zamfara, you remember Plateau? The same thing. The parties, because they did the wrong thing, they thought they could now steal through the candidates,” he said.
“And the law was very clear. Once you do that kind of thing, you cannot benefit from it. You are benefiting from it, if you are able to substitute a candidate.”
INEC’s position followed a recent Supreme Court ruling that affirmed the constitutionality of Sections 77(5), 77(6) and 77(7) of the Electoral Act 2026.
The court also upheld INEC’s revised timetable and schedule of activities for the 2027 general elections.
Under Section 77(5), only members whose names appear on a political party’s membership register submitted to INEC within the prescribed period can participate in the party’s primaries, congresses or conventions.
Section 77(6) requires parties to use the membership register submitted to INEC for their primaries, while Section 77(7) provides that a party that fails to submit its register within the stipulated period is not eligible to field candidates.
Since the Supreme Court’s judgement some candidates have been speculated in the media as having been affected. They include the APC governorship candidate in Rivers State, Kingsley Chinda and the NDC senatorial candidate for Delta Central, Ovie Omo-Agege, who is a former deputy senate president.
Mr Haruna said the commission’s position would apply to candidates across all elective positions, including the state Houses of Assembly.
“All the candidates, all the way to the Houses of Assembly, we interviewed them. If their names are not on the party register, they were not members of the party at the time that they contested for those tickets,” he said.
He said some political parties could consequently be left without candidates for some positions, depending on the outcome of INEC’s review.
“Some parties may not be able to finish with even governorship candidates,” he said.
The Supreme Court judgement followed a legal battle over provisions of the Electoral Act 2026 governing political party membership registers, party primaries and candidate nomination.
The Zenith Labour Party (ZLP) had challenged the provisions of sections 77(5), (6) and (7).
A Federal High Court judgement and a Court of Appeal decision initially nullified Sections 77(5) to (7) and Section 84(2), as well as aspects of INEC’s revised timetable for the 2027 elections, creating uncertainty over the commission’s timetable and the legal consequences of parties’ failure to comply with the membership-register requirements.
However, INEC appealed the decision at the Supreme Court, which subsequently set aside the Court of Appeal judgement and upheld the relevant provisions of the Electoral Act.
PREMIUM TIMES reported that the Supreme Court delivered the judgment on 24 September after hearing the appeal filed by the electoral commission against the Court of Appeal decision.
INEC Chairman, Joash Amupitan, said the commission only obtained the Certified True Copy (CTC) of the Supreme Court judgement on Tuesday.

title: 2027: We’ll also collate, share election results, ADC tells INEC
body: The African Democratic Congress (ADC) has declared that it will document, collate and share polling-unit results with the public during the 2027 general elections. The party said while it respects the Independent National Electoral Commission’s statutory responsibility to declare official election outcomes and to announce winners of elections, this wiill not stop it from documenting the process. In a statement by its National Publicity Secretary, Mallam Bolaji Abdullahi, the ADC said it decided to make its position known in response to the warning by the INEC Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan, against sharing of privately collated results. “We are aware of our rights to freedom of expression under the Constitution. We are also aware of the limitations associated with those rights. And we hold that our rights to collate and share election results are not abrogated by any of the limitation clauses.” “The ADC will share our collated results with the public. Our agents will document results, our structures will collate them, and we will communicate verified figures to the public, clearly identifying their source and status,” the party said. The party said although it recognises INEC’s responsibility to make official declarations of results and to declare winners of elections, that responsibility cannot abrogate the right of citizens to collect and collate election results and share them.

title: Bandits kill humanitarian worker in Sokoto attack
body: Suspected bandits have attacked a vehicle conveying humanitarian workers along the Kajiji-Shagari road in Sokoto State, killing one person and injuring two others. The incident occurred at about 7pm on Tuesday as the workers were returning to Sokoto after carrying out field operations in Tambuwal Local Government Area of the state. The deceased was identified as Ms Lydia Chinenye Nwankwo, a humanitarian and field operations professional who had worked with non-governmental and development organisations in Sokoto. Her younger sister, Victoria Nwankwo, confirmed her death to Daily Trust on Thursday, saying Lydia was shot in the chest during the attack. According to her, five people were travelling in the vehicle when the attackers opened fire on them. “My sister was shot on the chest, one of her colleagues was shot on the leg and another was brushed on the head by a bullet. The other people in the vehicle and the driver survived the attack. It is only my sister who died as a result of her injuries,” she said. Victoria said the family became worried when Lydia failed to return home and could not be reached by phone. She said a colleague later informed the family that the team had been attacked while returning from Tambuwal. According to her, Lydia’s body was eventually brought home in a Hilux vehicle at about 11pm, several hours after the attack. Her body was subsequently deposited at a morgue, she said. The Chairman of the Coalition of NGOs in Sokoto, Comrade Bello Shehu Gwadabawa, also confirmed that he was informed about the death but said he could not immediately provide details because he was out of town. He said the deceased was working with one of the development partners supporting the Sokoto State Ministry of Health. Meanwhile, the Sokoto State Police Command has confirmed an attack on some communities in Shagari Local Government Area, saying a police inspector also lost his life in the incident. The Command’s spokesman, DSP Ahmed Rufai, told Daily Trust that the Divisional Police Officer in charge of Shagari had briefed the state headquarters. Rufai, however, said the command was still collating information on the incident and could not immediately provide details on the extent of casualties and damage. “I just spoke with the DPO in charge of Shagari, who confirmed the attack on some communities in the local government. We are still on it. I cannot give details now until I gather my information about the incident. I will get back to you on it,” he said.

title: Lagos fire incidents claim 65 lives, destroy N13.2bn property
body: By Evelyn Usman LAGOS — No fewer than 65 persons were feared dead in fire and other emergency incidents across Lagos State between January and September 2026, while property estimated at N13.24 billion was lost, the Lagos State Fire and Rescue Service has said. The agency disclosed this in its Third Quarter Activity Report, which showed that it responded to 1,324 emergency incidents during the nine-month period. Of the total, 1,135 were fire incidents, while 210 victims were rescued alive and 65 suspected fatalities were recovered during emergency operations. According to the report, made available to Vanguard by the agency’s Senior Public Affairs Officer, Fadairo Maria, the incidents comprised 1,135 fire calls, 79 rescue calls, 100 salvage operations, nine collapsed-building incidents and one gas-related explosion. A monthly breakdown showed that January recorded the highest number of incidents with 203, followed by March with 201, while September recorded the lowest with 94 incidents. March also recorded the highest number of fire calls, with 176, followed by January with 173. September had the lowest number, with 80 fire calls. The Service disclosed that 341 false emergency calls were recorded during the period, warning that such calls could delay firefighters’ response to genuine emergencies and put lives and property at risk. The Controller-General of the Lagos State Fire and Rescue Service, Margaret Abimbola Adeseye, said the figures underscored the need for sustained fire-safety awareness, prompt reporting of emergencies and strict compliance with safety regulations. She urged residents to avoid indiscriminate burning, properly handle and store flammable materials, switch off and unplug electrical appliances when not in use, and avoid overloading electrical sockets. Adeseye also advised households, businesses and institutions to maintain functional fire extinguishers and ensure that escape routes and access points remained free of obstruction. N79.4bn property saved On the economic impact of the incidents, the Service said property estimated at N79.44 billion was saved, while losses stood at N13.24 billion. It put the total estimated value of property affected by the incidents at N92.68 billion. Adeseye warned that false emergency calls could have serious consequences for emergency response. “False emergency calls can delay the response of firefighters to genuine emergencies and potentially put lives, property and the environment at risk,” she said. She urged residents to report fire incidents promptly and cooperate with emergency responders whenever they arrive at incident scenes. The Controller-General reaffirmed the Service’s commitment to protecting lives and property through prompt emergency response, fire prevention, public enlightenment, enforcement of fire-safety standards and continuous engagement with communities. She stressed that “prevention remains the most effective way to reduce the devastating impact of fire emergencies.” The post Lagos fire incidents claim 65 lives, destroy N13.2bn property appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: New U.S. indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture
body:
Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores wave after his swearing-in ceremony for a third term at the National Assembly in Caracas, Venezuela, on Jan. 10, 2025. Ariana Cubillos/AP hide caption
NEW YORK — U.S. authorities added new torture charges Thursday to their case against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, ramping up pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking allegations.
Maduro and wife Cilia Flores, already charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., now also face allegations of human rights abuses during his time as president of the oil-rich South American nation.
The updated indictment "alleges conduct that is truly unthinkable," New York-based U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said outside the courthouse where the case is being handled. He said thousands of Venezuelans, and some Americans, were tortured to ensure that Maduro and Flores held onto power.
"This is the epitome of corruption," McDonald said.
The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest. Maduro, the indictment claims, signed off on torture methods, sought and got updates on specific victims' treatment, watched a video of a forced confession and personally threatened the killing of one prisoner's child "as a form of psychological torture."
Flores, a former legislator and attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment contends.
A message seeking comment was sent to Maduro's lawyer. Flores' attorney said he hadn't yet had time to review the new allegations.
The couple pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
They face potential sentences of life in prison if convicted.
Maduro, who served as Venezuela's president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied any wrongdoing.
Both Maduro and Flores have been behind bars in New York since early January, when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid. Flores' lawyers unsuccessfully asked a judge Thursday to release her on house arrest.
Outside the courthouse, over a dozen demonstrators chanted slogans and held signs supporting her request.
The revised indictment includes several mentions of the involvement of Venezuela's feared DGCIM military intelligence agency, which was headed for many years by one of Maduro's co-defendants, Gen. Hugo Carvajal. He broke with Maduro years ago, pleaded guilty last year to drug trafficking charges in New York and has offered to testify against his former boss.
While the indictment doesn't name the alleged torture victims, three are described as U.S. citizens. One was punched, subjected to electric shocks and forced to eat his own vomit during eight months of imprisonment, the indictment says. Another was beaten badly enough to necessitate a long hospital stay and had a gun stuck in his mouth. A third was handcuffed, hooded and beaten for two days every half an hour, suffering a permanent eye injury, the indictment said.
Maduro has long ignored lawsuits brought in U.S. courts by Americans who alleged they were beaten while in custody in Venezuela.
Among those who sued is Matthew Heath, a former U.S. Marine corporal from Tennessee. He was arrested at a roadblock in Venezuela in 2020 and held in custody for more than two years.
In May, Heath and another former prisoner won a $300 million default judgment against Maduro and other top Venezuelan officials for overseeing a pattern of torture. The lawsuit, brought under a federal anti-terrorism law, included allegations of waterboarding, electrocution, threats of rape with a nightstick, administration of mind-altering medications and the repeated use of a cramped cell nicknamed "El Tigrito."
"It's incredible to see a dictator in court," Heath said Thursday upon learning of the new charges. "The Maduro prosecution will do more to prevent the kidnapping of Americans by rogue regimes than a hundred press releases from the United Nations."
Meanwhile, Flores' lawyers argued that Flores, 69, has medical problems that cannot be treated effectively in jail. She has lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, might have suffered a minor heart attack in July, has "lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath" and has been told that she might need heart surgery, the attorneys said.
They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was "thrown against a wall or dresser" during her capture.
Prosecutors opposed the bail request, saying that Flores was an "extreme" flight risk and has been taken for treatment at a local hospital when needed.
U.S. District Court Judge Alvin Hellerstein denied Flores' request. He noted, among other things, that she's unwilling to undergo catheterization in jail in order to determine the cause of her heart problems and the appropriate steps for treatment.
He also pushed back at the notion that her high blood pressure was life threatening, noting she's already on medication for that.
U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a "surgical law enforcement operation." Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.

title: NPFL: Sporting Lagos Coach Buter fined N.5m over referee comments after Ikorodu City Derby
body:
Sporting Lagos head coach Jeffrey Buter has been fined N500,000 and cautioned by the Nigeria Premier Football League (NPFL) following an inquest into comments he made about refereeing after the Lagos derby against Ikorodu City.
The league imposed the sanction after Buter appeared before a disciplinary panel on Wednesday to explain his comments following Sporting Lagos’ goalless draw with Ikorodu City on 30 September.
The coach admitted before the panel that he was wrong to have made the statements during his post-match press interview, a concession which played a significant role in the relatively lenient punishment handed down by the NPFL.
Buter’s appearance before the panel followed a summons issued by the league after his comments attracted attention following the derby.
After Sporting Lagos were held to a 0-0 draw by Ikorodu City, Buter had questioned the standard of officiating and made comments suggesting that refereeing decisions were becoming an issue in the league.
The NPFL subsequently summoned the Sporting Lagos coach to explain his remarks, with the league warning against public statements capable of bringing the competition and its match officials into disrepute.
Following Wednesday’s inquest, the NPFL confirmed that Buter admitted he was in error during the press interview.
The league said his acknowledgement of wrongdoing, coupled with his relatively limited experience as a coach in the NPFL for the 2026/27 season, influenced the decision to impose a N500,000 fine rather than a more severe punishment.
In addition to the financial sanction, Buter was cautioned to refrain from making unsubstantiated public statements concerning the NPFL and its referees.
The league has given the Sporting Lagos coach seven working days to pay the fine, and failure to comply within the stipulated period could result in more stringent sanctions.
The latest decision also provided the NPFL with an opportunity to send a wider warning to coaches and club officials across the league.
The league urged participants to exercise greater restraint when speaking publicly about the competition, particularly when making claims or allegations that have not been formally substantiated.
According to the NPFL, reckless public statements have the potential to undermine the perception of the league in the eyes of supporters and the wider football public.
Rather than using post-match interviews or other public platforms to air grievances, coaches and club officials have been advised to make use of the league’s established dispute resolution mechanisms.
The NPFL stressed that official channels remain available to clubs and their representatives who wish to challenge decisions, raise complaints or seek redress over issues arising from matches.
For Buter, the N500,000 fine brings an end to the disciplinary proceedings arising from his comments, but the warning from the league is clear.
The Sporting Lagos coach has now been placed on notice to ensure that future criticism of the NPFL or its match officials is backed by evidence and channelled through the appropriate mechanisms rather than made through public statements.

title: Moscow Region Man Killed in Ukrainian Drone Attack
body:
A 57-year-old man was killed in the Moscow region town of Podolsk in a late afternoon Ukrainian drone attack, Moscow region Governor Andrei Vorobyov said Thursday.
The fatal incident occurred in the Klimovsk neighborhood of Podolsk some 40 kilometers (25 miles) south of Moscow.
A 37-year-old woman also sustained injuries during the attack.
Vorobyov said three vehicles also caught fire before firefighters extinguished the blaze, and window glass was shattered in a nearby residential apartment building.
Civil aviation authorities temporarily suspended arrivals and departures at Domodedovo, Vnukovo and Zhukovsky airports to ensure flight safety during the air raid alert.
In western Siberia’s Omsk region, Governor Vitaly Hotsenko said Ukrainian drones attacked a “northern industrial hub” after eyewitness reports indicated that Russia’s largest oil refinery was targeted.
