title: Ghana to lead ECOWAS adoption of Accra Convention on cargo documents – Trade Minister
body: Ghana is positioning itself to play a leading role in the adoption and implementation of the Accra Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents across the ECOWAS region. The Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Elizabeth Ofosu-Adjare, says Ghana is committed to signing and ratifying the United Nations Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents to help transform trade finance, cross-border commerce and digital cargo documentation. She made the commitment on Wednesday, October 7, 2026, when she opened a one-day virtual sensitisation programme on the Convention organised for ECOWAS Member States. The Convention was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on December 15, 2025, through Resolution 80/162 and is officially known as the United Nations Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents. It is also referred to as the Accra Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents. The new framework establishes common rules for the use of negotiable cargo documents in paper or electronic form for goods transported across different modes, including road, rail and air. It is intended to facilitate trade finance, the sale of goods in transit, multimodal transport and the digitalisation of international trade. Madam Ofosu-Adjare said the Convention presents an opportunity to address longstanding challenges associated with financing and trading goods transported by land and air, while strengthening regional trade and integration. She said the Convention will be opened for signature in Accra on October 26, 2026, making Ghana the host of a significant international treaty-signing event. The Minister described the sensitisation programme as an important opportunity for ECOWAS Member States to develop a common understanding of the Convention and assess its implications for trade and regional integration. She urged participating countries to examine the Convention against their respective national legal frameworks and return to their governments with clear recommendations on the way forward. Madam Ofosu-Adjare also expressed Ghana’s readiness to welcome ECOWAS Member States and stakeholders from around the world to Accra for the signing ceremony. The Secretary of the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL), Anna Joubin-Bret, and the Director of Trade at the ECOWAS Commission, Kolawole Sofola, encouraged Member States and other stakeholders to participate fully in the process. They called for stronger regional and international support for the Convention’s signature, ratification and effective implementation. The Convention will enter into force 180 days after the deposit of the tenth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.

title: 9.5m children received no routine vaccine in 57 countries in 2025 – Gavi
body:
Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, says 9.5 million children in 57 supported countries received no routine vaccine in 2025, despite gains in global immunisation.
The figure, described as the number of “zero-dose” children, was contained in Gavi’s 2025 Annual Progress Report, which reviewed the alliance’s 2021-2025 strategic period.
Gavi defines zero-dose children as infants who have not received the first dose of a diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis-containing vaccine by the end of their first year.
According to the report, the number of zero-dose children in 2025 was 600,000 lower than in 2024 and 25 per cent lower than the peak recorded in 2021 following disruptions to routine immunisation caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.
However, the figure remained four per cent above the 2019 baseline, partly because of continued growth in the number of children being born.
Gavi said children living in fragile, conflict-affected and humanitarian settings remain among those most likely to be missed by immunisation programmes.
Nigeria remains one of the countries with the highest number of zero-dose children. UNICEF estimated that about 2.2 million Nigerian children had never received a routine vaccine in 2025, the highest number in Africa.
The report highlighted Nigeria, Ethiopia and Pakistan among countries where emerging data showed stronger immunisation coverage gains in sub-national areas that received greater Gavi focus and investment during the 2021-2025 period.
Gavi said the findings underscored the value of targeted, equity-focused investments in reaching communities that are being missed by routine immunisation.
The report also identified Nigeria among countries covered by Gavi’s Zero-Dose Learning Hubs, which examined what works and what does not in identifying and reaching zero-dose and under-immunised children.
The findings from Nigeria, Bangladesh, Mali and Uganda highlighted several issues, including gender-related barriers to immunisation.
Despite the number of zero-dose children, Gavi said more than 73 million children were immunised through routine programmes with its support in 2025.
More than 351 million children were immunised during the 2021-2025 strategic period, “exceeding Gavi’s target of 300 million children.”
“By end 2025, Gavi-supported countries had immunised more than 1.3 billion unique children with Gavi support since 2000, exceeding our Investment Opportunity 2021-2025 commitment of more than 1.1 billion children immunised by 2025,” it noted.
Gavi said vaccination averted more than 2.2 million future deaths in 2025, bringing the total number of future deaths averted through its supported vaccination programmes to more than 7.8 million during the 2021-2025 period.
The report said immunisation programmes generated more than $30 billion in economic benefits for Gavi-supported countries in 2025, the highest amount recorded in a single year.
The benefits were calculated from the costs of illness averted, including medical and associated costs, caretaker wages and productivity losses resulting from disability or death.
Gavi said the programmes generated more than $104 billion in economic benefits between 2021 and 2025 and more than $308 billion between 2000 and 2025.
Countries also contributed a record $301 million towards the co-financing of Gavi-supported vaccines in 2025, an 18 per cent increase from 2024.
About 80 per cent of the contribution came from domestic resources, while “approximately 20 per cent from low-interest loans from the World Bank.”
Gavi said countries had contributed a total of $2.2 billion towards vaccine co-financing since the policy was introduced in 2008.
For its 2026 to 2030 strategic period, Gavi said it aims to protect another 500 million children through immunisation and avert between eight million and nine million future deaths.
The Alliance also targets more than $100 billion in economic benefits during the period. Gavi said it would place greater emphasis on reaching zero-dose and under-immunised children while strengthening the sustainability of national immunisation programmes.
In her comments, Gavi Chief Executive Officer, Sania Nishtar, said the results showed that immunisation generates benefits beyond preventing disease. “However, when it comes to immunisation we know that the return on investment extends far beyond health to supporting sustainable, inclusive economic growth,” Ms Nishtar said.
WHO Director-General, Tedros Ghebreyesus, also said immunisation delivers massive gains in lives saved and diseases prevented, but also in terms of economic benefits.
“Countries understand that the cost of failing to vaccinate is far too great, while the benefits extend across families, communities, economies and future generations,” Mr Ghebreyesus was quoted to have said.

title: Kano police arrest 47 suspects, recover drugs, weapons
body: By Hadiza Yusuf KANO — The Kano State Police Command has arrested 47 suspects for alleged thuggery, drug peddling, phone snatching and other related offences during operations conducted across the state between October 1 and 7, 2026. The Command also said it recovered quantities of suspected illicit drugs, dangerous weapons and three Android mobile phones allegedly snatched from victims. The Police Public Relations Officer, CSP Abdullahi Haruna Kiyawa, disclosed this in a statement on Thursday on behalf of the Commissioner of Police, CP Ibrahim Adamu Bakori. He said the arrests were made through intelligence-led and community-based policing operations conducted by different formations of the Command. In Panshekara, police surveillance teams carried out three separate operations and arrested 21 suspected drug dealers. The first operation led to the arrest of Abba Usman, 22, and Nasiru Hassan, 20, both of Panshekara Quarters. Police said the suspects were found with six sachets and 12 pieces of suspected Pregabalin capsules, as well as dried leaves suspected to be Cannabis sativa. In a separate operation, 11 suspects, led by 21-year-old Joel Munatuti of Samegu Quarters, were arrested with seven sachets of suspected Pregabalin, 439 tablets of suspected Exol, five pieces of suspected Diazepam and dried leaves suspected to be Cannabis sativa. Eight other suspects, led by 18-year-old Kelvin Friday of Yansama Quarters, were also arrested with six sachets of suspected Pregabalin, 43 tablets of suspected Exol and dried leaves suspected to be Cannabis sativa. Police also arrested 22-year-old Sadam Shuaibu of Yako Village, Kiru Local Government Area, on October 7. He was allegedly found with 105 wraps of dried leaves suspected to be Indian hemp and other substances suspected to be hard drugs. Police arrest suspected thugs In another operation at Hotoro Mahautar Gabas on October 4, police arrested 13 suspected thugs, popularly known as Yan Daba, following reports that the group was allegedly terrorising residents. According to the statement, items recovered from the suspects included 216 bottles of a substance identified by police as “Suck and Die,” six tubes of Red Sun Solution, four cutlasses, five axes, one sword, two gariyo, four knives, one hammer, two hacksaws, five sticks, three sharp iron rods, an MP3 radio, charms and four empty four-litre gallons. Similarly, operatives of the Anti-Kidnapping Squad arrested 10 suspected thugs on October 3 following information that a gang had gathered in large numbers around the Yan Yashi/Kofar Ruwa axis of Dala Local Government Area. The suspects were identified as Mohammed Usman, 30; Gaddafi Awaisu, 43; Abdulkarim Dalha, 22; Mustapha Isah, 19; Ibrahim Adam, 23; Abba Sale, 24; Ibrahim Rabi’u, 19; Abubakar Ibrahim, 24; Usman Hamisu, 25; and Ishimawi Sabo, 22. Police said the suspects were arrested in Kurna, Kofar Ruwa and Yan Yashi quarters, with swords, cutlasses, knives, sticks and clubs, as well as dried leaves suspected to be Indian hemp and other illicit drugs recovered from them. Two arrested over phone snatching Also on October 4, operatives of the Special Intervention Squad arrested two suspected phone snatchers, identified as Yaro Ahmad, 20, also known as Saisan, and Nafiu Almustapha, 20, also known as Small. The suspects were intercepted along Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital while allegedly operating with a tricycle. Three Android mobile phones suspected to have been snatched and the tricycle were recovered. According to the police, the suspects confessed during interrogation to dispossessing passengers of their phones through pickpocketing while conveying them to their destinations. The Command said all the suspects were undergoing discreet investigation at various police formations and would be charged to court upon completion of the investigations. title: Russia Says Checks Following Siberian Plague Lab Death Are Complete
body:
Russia said on Thursday it had completed health checks on all the contacts of a deceased lab worker at a plague research facility in Siberia, signaling a desire to draw a line under the affair.
Statements from the state health watchdog and the regional governor said monitoring of all the dead woman's contacts had concluded, and reiterated that no dangerous pathogens had been found in nearly 5,000 samples.
"Amidst intense media scrutiny, the specialists thoroughly investigated the situation. It was a test, but we passed it in worthy fashion," Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev said.
Yet despite pressure from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United States, Russian authorities have yet to state definitively whether the death of 28-year-old lab worker Darya Shipilova on Oct. 2 could have been caused by plague.
They have previously stated that she died from pneumonia but that the origin of the pneumonia had yet to be determined. They have also said she was appropriately vaccinated and that no microorganisms linked to her work were found in her body.
On Wednesday, senior WHO official Maria Van Kerkhove said the global body wanted more information from Russia on what laboratory tests had been conducted, which pathogens were evaluated and that "if this individual didn't die from plague, then how did she die?"
Russia says it has provided full information to the WHO according to established procedures.
Global health officials — as well as the world's media — have been particularly alert to pneumonia cases of undetermined cause since the Covid-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of fast-spreading fatal respiratory illness in China.
However, the cause of individual pneumonia cases can often not be determined.
The lung infection can have a variety of causes other than plague, including other bacterial infections or viral respiratory diseases, such as Covid or flu.

title: Driver of car attacked by occupation forces killed in Zaporizhia – Regional Military Administration
body:
Russian occupation forces struck a civilian vehicle in Zaporizhia, killing the driver instantly, said Mykhailo Semykin, head of Zaporizhia Regional Military Administration.
"The enemy has once again attacked civilians. A vehicle traveling along the road was hit. The car caught fire. Unfortunately, the driver died," he wrote on Telegram on Thursday.

title: Seventy-eight killed, 215 wounded in Russian strikes on Ukraine in recent days – Zelenskyy
body:
Russian strikes on Pryluky, Kramatorsk, Kyiv, and other Ukrainian cities in recent days have resulted in 78 deaths and 215 injuries, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported.
“I spoke with President of the European Council António Costa. I am grateful to António for his clear and principled stance in condemning Russian strikes against our people and for his condolences,” Zelenskyy said on X.
According to him, this represents a severe Russian escalation and terror directed against people and life itself. Zelenskyy emphasized the importance of leaders not ignoring the events unfolding in Ukraine.
The President also thanked Costa for the EUR 1.2 billion tranche received the day before. Zelenskyy stated that the funds would be used for Ukraine's defense, specifically for drones.
“We are working to secure other necessary decisions as well. We discussed the timeline for opening the next negotiating clusters, the winter energy package, and further financial support,” he noted.
Zelenskyy announced that he had agreed to hold a trilateral meeting with Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in the near future. Additionally, the head of state briefed the European Council President on upcoming contacts and meetings with the US side scheduled for the coming days; he noted that the Ukrainian delegation had already departed for these engagements.
As previously reported, European Council President António Costa, following a telephone conversation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, stated that he had invited the Ukrainian leader to the European Council meeting taking place next week in Brussels.

title: Bet9ja Foundation Empowers 350+ Young Nigerians at Third Edition of GEES to Earn, Build and Grow
body: Now in its third edition, GEES has continued to evolve with the changing realities facing young Nigerians. The inaugural edition in 2024 focused on employability and entrepreneurial success, while the second edition in 2025 explored the digital economy and preparing young people for the digital workspace . GEES 3.0 builds on that journey by taking the conversation further, from gaining skills and navigating the changing world of work to understanding how to earn, build and grow in today’s economy. This edition was delivered across three core tracks: Career, Wealth and Enterprise, giving participants practical perspectives on career positioning, global work opportunities, personal branding, wealth creation, investment and entrepreneurship. The summit brought together voices across careers, business and finance. Tomike Adeoye, award-winning entrepreneur, actor and media personality, delivered the Wealth Track keynote, while Dr. Solomon King, Capital Advisor and Executive Director of Lagos Angel Network, delivered the Career Track keynote. Speakers across the Wealth and Enterprise tracks further explored investment, venture building, business growth and entrepreneurship. A key highlight was the GEES Pitch Slam, which gave emerging entrepreneurs an opportunity to present their businesses, pitch their ideas and compete for prizes. Dharkag Foods emerged as the winner, with Savour Foods named first runner-up and Nail Luxe second runner-up. In total, more than ₦2.4 million worth of prizes and gifts was awarded to participants GEES 3.0 also created space for emerging career-focused ventures to demonstrate solutions directly to attendees. Entire Hire offered participants practical guidance on CV writing and interview preparation, including a demo interview experience designed to help candidates better position themselves for opportunities. Achieve Meter, an AI-powered career accelerator for professionals, graduates and students transitioning from school into the workforce, showcased how technology can support career development and positioning. “Earn. Build. Grow. captures an important reality for young people today. It is not enough to simply find a job; young people need the knowledge and confidence to earn, build something of their own and grow sustainably. The Pitch Slam is an important part of that vision because it gives young entrepreneurs more than visibility. It gives them a platform to present their ideas, receive recognition and access resources and feedback that can help their businesses.” said Ada Cuomo, Executive Director, Bet9ja Foundation. “GEES is about meeting young people where they are and giving them something they can take away and use. Whether that is a clearer career direction, a stronger business pitch or a better understanding of how to build wealth, we want every participant to leave knowing what their next move can be,” said Omotola Oronti, Marketing Manager, Bet9ja Foundation. For one returning participant, GEES has become a space where learning and meaningful connections happen side by side. Having attended the previous edition, she returned for GEES 3.0 and reflected on how the experience had evolved. “I attended GEES last year and I also came this year because I really enjoyed the experience. Last year, the conversations around the digital economy opened my mind to the opportunities available in the changing world of work. This year felt like the next step, it was more about what I can actually do with the knowledge, how I can position myself for career growth, build something of my own and create more opportunities for myself. I also got to meet Tomike Adeoye, someone I have looked up to in the media space, which made the experience even more memorable.” From its first edition in 2024, through its focus on the digital economy in 2025, to “Earn. Build. Grow.” in 2026, GEES continues to evolve around one central goal: helping young Nigerians move from potential to opportunity. Through GEES and its wider Youth Empowerment initiatives, Bet9ja Foundation continues to create platforms that help young Nigerians earn, build and grow. About Bet9jaFoundation Bet9ja Foundation is a philanthropic organization committed to improving lives and creating opportunities for people and communities across Nigeria. Through programmes focused on education, healthcare, youth empowerment, sports, and community development, the Foundation works to address real needs and support lasting progress. Driven by the belief that opportunity can transform lives, Bet9ja Foundation continues to invest in initiatives that empower individuals, strengthen communities, and make a meaningful difference where it matters most. title: Middle East economy to shrink 2.1% in 2026, Gulf economies by 4.3%, World Bank forecasts
body: The economies of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan region are projected to contract by 2.1% in 2026, with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states expected to be hit harder, contracting by an average of 4.3%, according to a new World Bank report released on Tuesday.Qatar and Kuwait are expected to be the hardest-hit GCC economies, with GDP forecast to contract by 20.9% and 14.6%, respectively, in 2026. The United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia are projected to be the least affected among GCC members, with their economies forecast to contract by 1.6% and 2.0%, respectively.Qatar's economy, facing its weakest growth forecast in decades, has been heavily affected by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Average monthly natural gas production in Qatar fell by approximately 67% between March and July 2026, compared to the same period in 2025.Gulf oil production collectively has fallen from around 26 million barrels per day before to around 16 million bpd in March, according to the World Bank.The disruption has also driven inflation higher across the Gulf. Qatar's food inflation exceeded 12% year-on-year as of June, while average overall inflation remained at around 2%. In Bahrain and Oman, food inflation surpassed 7%, while headline inflation [overall increase] stood at around 3%.Iraq, Iran face sharp GDP declines as oil production falls and inflation surgesIn Iraq and Iran, GDP is forecast to decline by 12.4% and 7.7%, respectively, with both countries operating at just 55% to 70% of their estimated oil production capacity. In Iran, inflation has also surged, rising from around 32% in mid-2024 to 89% in August 2026, according to World Bank figures.Lebanon has also felt the economic impact of the conflict, although its inflation rate has eased from the sharp rise seen during the early months of the war and currently stands above 15%.Gasoline prices have risen by at least 40% in Lebanon, while diesel prices have increased by over 80%. Fuel prices in the West Bank and Gaza have also risen by more than 40%.Oil-importing economies have proved more resilient, with regional growth expected to reach 4.3% in 2026, compared with 3.9% in 2025.However, importing countries, like Egypt, Jordan, Morocco, Pakistan, and Tunisia, remain vulnerable to the economic fallout of the conflict. They face higher inflation as oil and other commodity prices rise, reduced fiscal room, potentially lower remittances from Gulf economies, and higher borrowing costs, driven in part by increased insurance risk premiums as the conflict continues.World Bank forecasts 7.8% regional economic rebound in 2027 if conflict endsExcluding Iran, the World Bank Group macroeconomic models projected that, if the conflict were to end this year, regional economies would rebound sharply, to 7.8% in 2027, driven by a recovery in hydrocarbon production, the normalization of trade routes, and base effects.The global economy was able to absorb much of the shock from the blockade, the World Bank noted, as pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the UAE bypassed the disruption and brought an additional 2.8 million bpd to global markets. Brazil, Kazakhstan, Venezuela, and the United States also continued exporting, while inventories helped make up shortfalls, and global demand fell by an estimated 5.8 million bpd compared with pre-conflict levels.World Bank warns extreme weather could worsen food shortages across the regionWhile the impact of the blockade has so far remained manageable for most countries, the World Bank warned that El Niño could pose an additional threat to food security across the region, where families are already facing risks from declining humanitarian aid funding.Alongside Pakistan and Afghanistan, which are directly exposed through changing monsoon conditions and heat stress, the World Bank warned that Egypt, Iraq, and Tunisia needed close monitoring given existing water stress.

title: Major internet outage hits Russia after strike on Yandex data center
body:
The Moscow Times reported this, according to Ukrinform.
According to the monitoring portals Sboy.rf and Downdetector, Russian banking services, online platforms, mobile operators, retail websites and Russian Railways services have experienced disruptions. Users reported problems with the services of several banks, as well as Google, YouTube, RuTube, Ivi, KION and Dnevnik.ru. The most complaints were recorded about Avito, with more than 14,000 reports in the past 24 hours.
According to Downdetector, the most serious problems are being reported in St. Petersburg and Moscow.
The outages began after an attack on a Yandex data center in Sasovo, Ryazan region, which caused a fire. Following the incident, users reported problems with Yandex Disk, Yandex Documents and other services.
The attack also caused problems with online bus ticket sales in the Moscow region. Mostransavto attributed the disruptions to the shutdown of the data center that supported the relevant services and said it could take up to 24 hours to restore the system.
In addition, users reported difficulties accessing the websites of Russian media outlets, including RBC, RIA Novosti, Kommersant, Vedomosti, Interfax and Vesti. Some of the sites were also inaccessible via VPN.
As reported by Ukrinform, overnight into October 8, drones struck an oil refinery in Bashkortostan and a data center belonging to Russia’s most popular mapping service, Yandex, in the Ryazan region.

title: The imagination that began it all: The Persian-Jewish poet bringing Genesis back to life - opinion
body: As the annual cycle of Torah reading begins anew, Israeli readers once again find themselves facing the story of Creation. We have known it since childhood: from Bible classes and ceremonies to debates on faith versus science and countless commentaries. Yet, precisely because of this deep familiarity, it can seem as though no surprises remain. The world was created, humanity was placed at its center, Eden was sealed – and we move on.Yet centuries ago, at the far end of the Jewish world, a poet named Shahin Shirazi dared to do what we often struggle to do today: inject risk, color, and imagination back into a familiar narrative. This was not imagination as mere decoration, but as a driving force allowing us to re-examine the foundational roots of human culture.Shahin, who lived in 14th-century Persia, was one of Persian Jewry's greatest and most daring creators. He was not simply a poet writing on Jewish themes; he was an artist who constructed an entire cultural worldview – deeply Jewish in its roots, Persian in its aesthetic language, and Middle Eastern in the scope of its imagery. His monumental oeuvre included expansive epics, among them poetic cycles dedicated to Moses, Ezra, Esther, and the Creation. His final masterpiece, Genesis-Nama, marked his most mature work – a tapestry where memory, faith, Midrash, and fantasy converge within a single vision.The work of Shahin ShiraziShahin's adoption of the Persian epic form was by no means accidental. He understood that stories do not survive on content alone; they live through rhythm, music, metaphor, and the heroic figures that stir a culture's soul. He harnessed the artistic tools of his environment in service of Jewish memory. He did so neither apologetically nor to assimilate, but out of a profound conviction that Judaism could engage with Iran's great cultural landscape and speak there in its own distinct voice.This is not merely a literary question; it is a profoundly Israeli one: Does an identity gain strength by filtering out every external influence, or by encountering another culture without losing its own essence?In Shahin's work, Adam is not merely a naive creature who falls. He is a figure of cosmic, almost majestic stature. The Patriarchs and leaders do not appear as static figures from a textbook, but as heroes endowed with radiance, responsibility, and a sense of destiny. Shahin reminds us of a truth that Israeli discourse often forgets: tradition is not a museum exhibit. It is a living canvas, and every generation possesses the right – perhaps even the duty – to clothe it in the imagery through which it thinks and feels.One of the most compelling concepts in his work concerns the tension between fire and earth. Azazel, created from fire and light, looks upon the human being formed from earth and concludes that a creature's material origins dictate its worth. To him, fire appears superior: bright, intense, impressive, and immediate. Earth, by contrast, seems humble, heavy, and devoid of glory. Shahin subverts this perspective. Earth is that which sustains, receives, nurtures, and carries life. Fire consumes itself; earth enables others to be born.This message resonates far beyond theology. We live in an era that worships the immediate and the flashy: power, speed, virality, victory, and visibility. Whatever makes an instant impression is valued over that which is built patiently over time. Shahin proposes a different hierarchy of values: a thing's worth is not defined by its brilliance, but by its capacity to contain and nurture. The loudest voice in the room is not necessarily the strongest; true strength often belongs to those capable of sustaining life even when it is complex, slow, and unphotogenic.This is also a vital lesson in humility. The tragic flaw is not merely a rebellion against a command, but a failure of vision. Anyone who sees only the physical material from which a human being was formed misses the divine breath placed within them. Anyone who judges people solely by their origins, status, or appearance fails to recognize their inner potential. In this sense, Shahin's Azazel is strikingly contemporary: he falls because he knows how to categorize, but lacks the ability to imagine.Even the Garden of Eden in Shahin's work is not a product of simple nostalgia for a bygone paradise. Wheat becomes a symbol of knowledge hard-won through labor, persistence, craftsmanship, and the transformation of nature into culture. This offers an almost Zionist imagery of knowledge: not an instantaneous revelation from the heavens, but wisdom acquired through dedicated effort. Human partnership, too, is presented not as an abstract ideal, but as the capacity to build a life together within physical bounds, time, and human limitations. Perfection is not found in a pure spirit hovering above the world, but in a bond that manages to endure within it.Here lies Shahin's unique relevance for Israel today. For decades, we have relied on a narrow narrative of Jewish culture: East versus West, tradition versus modernity, Israeliness versus Diaspora. Shahin dismantles these dichotomies. He reminds us that Judaism can be profound without being closed, faithful to itself without being defensive, and Middle Eastern without apology.Moreover, he brings to center stage a chapter long relegated to the margins: the Jews of Iran. This is not merely a community that survived, nor simply a diaspora to be recalled on memorial days. It is a vibrant spiritual world that created, renewed, and imagined, bestowing an epic language upon our foundational stories. It is an integral part of the Jewish home, not an afterthought.In this context, it is essential to acknowledge the dedicated individuals and patrons of culture who work faithfully to preserve and transmit Persian-Jewish heritage through the “Bama Tova” organization (www.bamatova.org). Thanks to key supporters and families, such as the Ganji family and the Mahfar family, this rich heritage does not remain locked in an archive. It continues to breathe, reach the next generation, and claim its rightful place within Israeli culture. Heritage does not preserve itself; it relies on those who believe in it, invest in it, and carry it forward.As we open the Book of Genesis once again, perhaps we should not rush toward familiar debates over literal interpretation versus Midrash, faith versus science, or past versus present. Instead, we might ask a simpler question: What do we choose to see when we look at a human being? Do we see only earth – weakness, origins, and physical matter – or do we see the capacity to turn matter into a vessel for life?Shahin does not call on us to return to medieval Persia. He invites us to return to the creative imagination from which all creation begins – the fundamental power that enables us to see possibility where others see only raw material, history, or limitation. In an Israel where everything seems to have already been said about Genesis, imagination may be the newest way to begin the year.The writer is a scholar of cultures and religions, liturgical poet, filmmaker, and director of the “Bama Tova” organization.
